entry.title: Classic UK climb: Dunkery Beacon
entry.content:
Cyclist
Classic UK climb: Dunkery Beacon

It’s not always obvious where a climb starts. For example, a couple of issues ago Cyclist’s deputy editor, James Spender, began his description of The Tumble in Wales by offering four potential starting points. In contrast, the start of the climb up to Dunkery Beacon in Somerset is in no doubt.

Give way lines at the junction on the road between Crook Horn Hill and Chisland Drive demarcate it as clearly as a race start line. If that wasn’t enough, another clue is that the gradient tips up to 16% immediately as if someone has gripped the road, pressed their thumbs into it and bent it like a length of pipe cleaner. Be sure to shift into a low gear before you turn the corner, otherwise your poor derailleur will be forced to crunch and grind your chain up the cassette as you try desperately to keep the pedals turning.

The road snakes its way up through dense woodland initially, the trees forming a gloomy tunnel over tarmac in such good nick that anywhere else it would be a joy to ride on. Here, however, the smooth surface is made greasy by leaf litter and the lack of sunlight, meaning you need to contend with the extra challenge of stopping your back wheel from spinning out on a gradient that’s almost impossible to remain seated on.

A cattle grid pitched at 12% provides a little extra spice a few hundred metres in, but if you make it past that without incident your reward is a gradual lessening in the incline. By the lookout spot of Webber’s Post it has dissipated entirely and the road is flat for a couple of hundred metres.

It’s just as well you’ve been afforded the opportunity to stop chewing your stem: the area is famed for its views out across Horner’s Woods, where an oak tree that’s more than 5,000 years old resides. It’s also an access point to some of the 250km of trails and bridleways that criss-cross the Holnicote Estate, making this part of Exmoor just as good for gravel and mountain biking as it is for road riding.

Article continues below…

A gift that keeps giving

The Holnicote Estate makes up over 12,000 acres of the Exmoor National Park, with much of it having been donated to the National Trust by the family that has owned it since the 1700s. In 1944 the Trust was gifted almost 10,000 acres in one go, which remains one of the largest donations ever given to the organisation. This followed an initial 860 acres in the 1930s, when a large cairn was erected on the site of a Bronze Age burial mound to commemorate the donation.

That cairn marks the highest point on Exmoor and sits on the top of Dunkery Beacon, which is itself the top of Dunkery Hill and can be visited via a gravel track that starts at the summit of this road climb. But first you have to finish the climb, and from Webber’s Post there’s still another 2km to go.

As the tree cover comes to an end, the steepness begins to ramp upward once more. It’s a much steadier increase this time, percent by percent as the road scythes between the scrubby bushes. By the time you reach a chicane almost tight enough to be a pair of switchbacks, the gradient is back in the high teens, but try to take advantage of the road swinging to the left and right to glance over your shoulder at an impressive view over Porlock and the Bristol Channel to the south coast of Wales. It’s the only opportunity you’ll get to do it, because after those bends the road straightens and heads directly up onto the moors proper.

The views are more open left and right now. The plunging hills are impressive but a moors-influenced microclimate here can turn a sunny summer’s day overcast and chilly very quickly. If that’s the case, your surroundings become bleak and it’s hard not to feel isolated and vulnerable, such is the remoteness of Exmoor.

Provided mist doesn’t obscure your view, the rest of the climb is laid bare ahead, so it’s a case of avoiding the ponies that have free rein of this area, settling into a rhythm and winching to the top as the gradient peters out as steadily as it ramped up after Webber’s Post.

When it arrives, the summit is just a layby opposite the gravel track that leads to the cairn at Dunkery Beacon. It’s a finish that’s as obscure as the start was definite, but the panoramic views out over Exmoor make it memorable all the same.

The stats

Location Exmoor National Park, Somerset
Length 3.1km
Summit height 449m
Ascent 334m
Average gradient 10%
Maximum gradient 20%
Current best Strava time
KoM Andrew Feather, UK, 10min 05sec
QoM Illi Gardner (pro), UK, 13min 52sec

entry.title: The 2027 selection of premium winter cycling kit
entry.content:
Cyclist
The 2027 selection of premium winter cycling kit

Unlike the simplicity of summer – lightweight jersey, bibshorts, done – winter kit has always had its work cut out. An early start that’s dark and bitter might morph into a windy and rainy mid-morning, which gives over to sunny spells by early afternoon. 

Luckily technical fabric development continues apace, and this season’s garments are more proficient than ever at keeping the rider dry, warm and comfortable now that summer is officially over.

Items such as Assos’s Mille GT Spring Fall and Endura’s AllTrack long-sleeve jerseys look ideal for clement rides where breathability takes priority. When the conditions take a turn for the worse, there are options such as the Sphere Gore-Tex Jacket from Portal and Universal Colours’ three-layer Mono Rain Jacket. Visibility-boosting bibtights from Kostüme and specialist shoes from Lake ensure your lower half is well catered for as well, so read on to find out more about this winter’s best kit.

Winter kit brands in this guide

• Assos
• Kostüme
• GripGrab
• Endura
• Lake
• Portal
• Universal Colours
• Santini
• Bioracer
• Pactimo

Assos

Him

  • Assos Mille GT Spring Fall Jersey S11, £165, buy now at assos.com
  • Assos Mille GT Spring Fall Bibtights S11, £185, buy now at assos.com
  • Assos Spring Fall Gloves P1, £75, buy now at assos.com

With an updated fit to allow more room across the chest for the more upright position adopted for endurance rides, the Mille GT Jersey is the perfect companion on cooler rides. Other clever details include Assos’s zeroPressure waist, to keep the Mille GT in place without constricting the stomach area, and Triple Ramp Pockets, where flexible panels create a lid-style closure to keep contents secure and protect against the elements. Like the bibtights, the Mille GT Jersey is designed to work down to around 12°C.

‘That mid-weight insulation comes from RX fabric on the body and arms, which offers good insulation, is fast-drying and very breathable,’ Assos says. ‘The close, supportive cut also means the Mille layers up really well with our windproof and waterproof shells for maximum protection.’

Her

  • Assos Mille GT Spring Fall Jersey S11, £165, buy now at assos.com
  • Assos Women’s Skin Layer P1 Short Sleeve Base Layer, £75, buy now at assos.com
  • Assos Uma GT Spring Fall Bibtights S11, £185, buy now at assos.com
  • Assos Spring Fall Gloves P1, £75, buy now at assos.com

Assos’s take on spring-autumn endurance kit is simple: make it warm, comfortable and streamlined.

‘It’s designed for superior comfort on training rides and sustained efforts on long rides in cooler conditions,’ Assos tells us. ‘The seatpad in the Uma GT tights is super-comfortable on long distances thanks to 12mm high-density foam and anatomy-specific shaping to reduce chafing, and uses Assos’s goldenGate 2.0 stitching, where the pad isn’t stitched along the sides to allow it to better move with the body when pedalling. 

‘Then there’s the fabrics. We use a new textile from Polar, which has a thermoregulating warp knit that offers mid-weight insulation – down to 12°C – breathability and a four-way stretch for targeted muscle support, but is made from over 50% recycled polyamide.’

Kostüme

Him

  • Kostüme Signature Unisex Ponytail Cap, £35, buy now at kostume.cc
  • Kostüme Signature Neck Warmer, £30, buy now at kostume.cc
  • Kostüme Windproof Cargo Gilet, £155, buy now at kostume.cc
  • Kostüme Winter Long-Sleeve Cargo Jersey, £175, buy now at kostume.cc
  • Kostüme Signature Sleeveless Base Layer, £40, buy now at kostume.cc
  • Kostüme Deep Winter Bibshorts, £230, buy now at kostume.cc

If the words ‘indoor training’ fill you with dread, then Kostüme’s Deep Winter Bibshorts might be just the ticket. 

They can deal with sustained downpours as well as freezing temperatures thanks to a sturdy Italian two-layer softshell that’s fully waterproof, breathable and PFAS-free. Down below, the four-layer chamois pad uses memory foam to ensure you stay both comfortable and dry, and it is also layered with an aloe-infused microfibre surface that performs a similar role to chamois cream.

‘They borrow the same membrane fabric as our winter tights, meaning they are totally weatherproof,’ says Ed Bartlett, Kostüme’s founder. ‘They are absolutely perfect for those chilly wet and windy days when tights would be too much but normal bibs would not be enough, and they will literally not wet out.’

Her

  • Kostüme Signature Unisex Ponytail Cap, £35, buy now at kostume.cc
  • Kostüme Signature Neck Warmer, £30, buy now at kostume.cc
  • Kostüme Windproof Cargo Gilet, £155, buy now at kostume.cc
  • Kostüme Winter Long-Sleeve Cargo Jersey, £175, buy now at kostume.cc
  • Kostüme Signature Long-Sleeve Base Layer, £65, buy now at kostume.cc
  • Kostüme Deep Winter Bibtight, £285, buy now at kostume.cc

As proof of concepts go, having a world record breaker wear your jersey from one end of a continent to the other isn’t half bad. Ultra-rider Sarah Ruggins did just that when she rode from the bottom of Spain to the top of Norway – 6,000km – in just under 14 days, using Kostüme products including the Winter Long-sleeve Cargo Jersey for much of the ride.

‘The fine-gauge Italian double-knit fabric gives it natural wind-stopping capability and very good venting,’ says Bartlett. ‘The jersey has brushed-back sleeves so you can wear it with a sleeveless base layer in milder weather or switch to a long-sleeve base layer and our Cargo Gilet when it’s really cold.’

Kostüme operates a pre-order model that cuts waste, meaning you can only buy this collection from 25th September until 11th October.

GripGrab

Him

  • GripGrab PACR Thermal Long Sleeve Jersey, £126, buy now at gripgrab.com
  • GripGrab PACR Thermal Bibtights, £160, buy now at gripgrab.com
  • GripGrab Winter Seamless Long Sleeve Base Layer, £75, buy now at gripgrab.com

Available in six autumnal colours, the PACR Thermal Long Sleeve Jersey sits in the sweet spot between performance and comfort.

‘The whole PACR line is for people who want to feel fast,’ says Sophie Goetz, senior product developer for GripGrab. ‘It’s a race fit, and for warmth and insulation we use a microfleece fabric that uses a really tight knit that gives you a certain amount of wind protection. On the inside the microfleece is really soft, and the brushed surface gives you a warm feeling. On the outside there’s a DWR treatment to give you some protection from damp – maybe not rain but spray from the road.’

The neat fit means it can be used as a mid-layer for when it’s really cold – ‘Below 0°C I wear it with a winter jacket over the top,’ says Goetz – or on its own with a base layer on autumn days when temperatures are around 7°-14°C.

Her

  • GripGrab PACR Winter Jacket, £200, buy now at gripgrab.com
  • GripGrab PACR Thermal Bibtights, £160, buy now at gripgrab.com
  • GripGrab Women’s Merino Blend Thermal Long Sleeve Base Layer, £70, buy now at gripgrab.com

Designed for temperatures down to 0°C, GripGrab’s PACR (pronounced ‘pacer’) Thermal Bibtights use a Superroubaix fabric that offers a lot of stretch.

‘This provides a soft compression that gives great comfort but also plenty of freedom of movement,’ says Goetz. ‘When you put them on they just feel great.’

As well as excellent breathability, the bibs have a DWR coating for protection, and the right leg has a side pocket that can store a phone or other essentials.

‘It uses a really strong woven fabric so you can put a lot of things in it,’ says Goetz, ‘but when it’s not in use it sits so flat you don’t even know it’s there.’

On the inside is an Elastic Interface pad with women-specific shaping and a dense foam for long-term comfort. 

Endura

Him

  • Endura FS260 Mips Helmet, £120, buy now at endurasport.com
  • Endura Men’s AllTrack Ride Long-Sleeve Jersey, £115, buy now at endurasport.com
  • Endura Men’s FS260 Thermo Bibtights II, £120, buy now at endurasport.com
  • Endura SingleTrack Windproof Gloves, £36, buy now at endurasport.com

As the name suggests, the AllTrack Ride Jersey is made to take on all tracks, for riders combining road and gravel in changeable conditions – something we Brits know all too well.

‘It’s for any terrain, with the focus mainly on gravel,’ says Ilma Barbaroviciute, UK community manager for Endura. ‘In the cycling world it’s described as a “relaxed” fit, so not as aero as a road jersey but not super-baggy like mountain bike kit.’

The main body of the jersey is a merino blend fabric for comfort and temperature regulation, while the sleeves are made from a stretchy rip-stop fabric for ease of movement and protection from scratches and scrapes.

‘Endura gear is built to last,’ says Barbaroviciute, ‘so you can buy it in the knowledge that you won’t have to replace it after a season. The watch words are durability and relaxability – if that’s even a word.’ It is now.

Her

  • Endura Women’s AllTrack Ride Long-Sleeve Jersey, £115, buy now at endurasport.com
  • Endura Women’s Pro SL Bibtights, £200, buy now at endurasport.com
  • Endura SingleTrack Windproof Gloves, £36, buy now at endurasport.com

Endura describes its Pro SL Bibtights as ‘the most technically advanced bibtights we have ever produced’. The main leg panels are four-way stretch, windproof, water-repellent, breathable and come with a soft, brushed inner face for warmth and comfort. The front section around the torso is a panel of high-wicking material that is more supportive and comfortable than straps, while a cunning overlap at the knee allows for unrestricted articulation.

The insert is Endura’s top-of-the-range 800-Series pad. This includes a medical grade elastomer, as used in prosthetics, to offer greater protection in sensitive areas. 

‘But probably my favourite feature is the DropSeat,’ says Barbaroviciute, ‘as it makes stopping for a nature break easy without taking off the bibs.’

Lake

  • Lake MXZ21, £250, buy now at lakecycling.com

Lake boasts high-performance winter-specific options for off-road as well. 

‘The MXZ21’s carbon midsole makes it well suited to performance-oriented riding where stiffness and power transfer remain important, but additional protection from cold and wet conditions is needed,’ says Christian Van Asten, Lake’s owner. ‘The real-rubber outsole also makes it practical when you need to get off the bike on wet or slippery surfaces.’

The MXZ21 forgoes a Boa closure in favour of speed laces: ‘They complement the shoe’s approach. Rather than needing several small adjustments, one pull cinches the upper around the foot, making entry and removal quick and straightforward when your hands are cold. It also helps make the shoe the lightest winter option in our range,’ says Van Asten.

  • Lake CX146, £225, buy now at lakecycling.com

The benefits of dedicated winter shoes are well known. Versus a summer shoe and overshoe combo, they offer more consistent weather protection and insulation.

‘One of the biggest advantages of the CX146, though, is fit choice,’ says Van Asten. ‘It’s available in both regular and wide – a winter shoe that’s too tight can restrict circulation and make cold feet worse. By offering different options we allow enough space for an appropriate winter sock without sacrificing foot security.’

The CX146 has a low bulk construction, so together with the stiff nylon sole and three-bolt cleat pattern, it retains the feel of a cycling shoe.

‘The Boa M4 closure is another key detail,’ says Van Asten. ‘It has been designed to be large enough to operate while wearing gloves.’

Portal

Him

  • Portal Trade Winds Helmet, £260, buy now at portal-brand.com
  • Portal Sphere Gore-Tex Jacket, £395, buy now at portal-brand.com
  • Portal Range Light Jersey, £145, buy now at portal-brand.com
  • Portal Realm Cargo Short 2.0, £265, buy now at portal-brand.com
  • Portal Drift Merino Gaitor, £40, buy now at portal-brand.com
  • Portal Drift Merino Gloves, £50, buy now at portal-brand.com

Portal’s Sphere Gore-Tex Jacket is designed to be versatile for wearing on or off the bike, and uses technical materials to achieve a light 173g weight and a waterproof layer that can also breathe.

‘After Gore-Tex’s Shakedry was discontinued we didn’t think this material could compete, but it does,’ says Portal’s co-founder John Roberts. ‘We’ve tested it extensively and there’s a noticeable difference in breathability compared to other three-layer materials on the market. 

‘Gore-Tex innovates in performance and sustainability, and we were delighted to get a licence to use its PFAS-free material.’

To maximise adjustability there’s a drawstring hem and a pleat at the rear to allow space for a cargo vest to be worn underneath – plus it stuffs neatly into a concealed zipped pocket that doubles as a stash for valuables. 

Her

  • Portal Trade Winds Helmet, £260, buy now at portal-brand.com
  • Portal Range Light Jersey, £145, buy now at portal-brand.com
  • Portal Sphere Gore-Tex Jacket, £395, buy now at portal-brand.com
  • Portal Realm Cargo 2.0 Bibshorts, £265, buy now at portal-brand.com
  • Portal Drift Merino Gaitor, £40, buy now at portal-brand.com
  • Portal Drift Merino Gloves, £50, buy now at portal-brand.com
  • Portal Pattern Active Socks, £20, buy now at portal-brand.com

Storage, durability and comfort are three key components of the Portal Realm Cargo 2.0 Bibshorts. As well as thigh storage there are five other pockets dotted around the waist area to free up your jersey, plus Portal uses abrasion-resistant Dyneema yarns to make them extra-sturdy.

‘This second generation takes everything we loved about the first version – pockets, integrated thigh gripper and honeycomb fabric on the thighs for wicking – while improving the fit and making the short nearly twice as light,’ says Roberts. 

‘The chamois is more minimal, there’s a lightweight stretch woven fabric in the main body and a lighter-weight Dyneema weave in the thigh and stomach pockets. Once you’ve used the stomach pockets on a bibshort it’s hard to go back to a pair without them.’

Universal Colours

Him

  • Universal Colours Mono Rain Jacket, £220, buy now at universalcolours.com
  • Universal Colours Men’s Mono Bibtights, £165, buy now at universalcolours.com
  • Universal Colours Men’s Mono Long-Sleeve Jersey, £125, buy now at universalcolours.com
  • Universal Colours Men’s Mono Sleeveless Base Layer, £45, buy now at universalcolours.com
  • Universal Colours Merino Winter Socks, £20, buy now at universalcolours.com

If there’s one item riders will be packing on most winter rides, it’s a rain shell. Handily, Universal Colours’ Mono Rain Jacket not only packs down easily into a jersey pocket but packs a performance punch too.

‘We’ve used a premium Japanese PU membrane and a PFAS-free DWR coating to deliver fully waterproof and breathable protection,’ says Tom Webb, creative lead at Universal Colours.

‘It has a three-layer construction with taped seams and a two-way Aquaguard zip to create a really reliable weather barrier.’

The Mono jacket is available in a choice of six colours, and has been designed with a svelte, shorter cut to keep everything neat and aerodynamic
while riding, so it won’t slow you down while it’s keeping you dry.

Her

  • Universal Colours Mono Rain Jacket, £220, buy now at universalcolours.com
  • Universal Colours Women’s Mono Bibtights, £165, buy now at universalcolours.com
  • Universal Colours Women’s Mono Long-Sleeve Jersey, £125, buy now at universalcolours.com
  • Universal Colours Men’s Mono Sleeveless Base Layer, £45, buy now at universalcolours.com

Universal Colours uses a highly stretchy recycled Italian nylon to maximise freedom of movement in its bibtights, which the brand says are warm enough to ride down to 3°C. There are separate designs for men and women, with anatomically specific chamois pads to ensure that riders can stay comfortable for longer. A rear zip on the women’s bibs also help with nature breaks.

‘We partnered with Elastic Interface and fitted a women-specific multi-density pad with perforated 13mm thick foam for high levels of vibration damping,’ says Webb. 

‘The nylon we chose as our main material has a brushed back for comfort and warmth, plus it has a PFAS-free plant-based DWR coating to repel moisture.’

Santini

Him

  • Santini RTR Jacket, £160, buy now at santinicycling.com
  • Santini Dry LS Base Layer, £60, buy now at santinicycling.com
  • Santini RTR Bibtights, £130, buy now at santinicycling.com
  • Santini Puro Socks, £16, buy now at santinicycling.com

Santini’s Ready To Ride collection focuses on simplicity and quality, and the RTR Jacket is a good example of the kit’s approach.

The brand’s latest winter product uses a three-layer membrane to protect against all but the worst weather yet combines that with fleece inserts to ensure the garment provides comfort and freedom of movement.

‘The jacket has a high collar for extra protection, triple rear pockets and reflective details, so can be used in grotty weather between -5°C and +5°C, says Santini’s co-owner and marketing director Paola Santini. 

Importantly, the jacket uses a dyed garment technique, whereby it’s produced in white and then dyed afterwards, which helps improve the vibrancy and durability of the colour, helping the rider stand out in winter conditions for an extra layer of safety.

Her

  • Santini RTR Jacket, £160, buy now at santinicycling.com
  • Santini Dry LS Base Layer, £60, buy now at santinicycling.com
  • Santini RTR Bibtights, £130, buy now at santinicycling.com

Though garment styling and colours are mirrored between male and female options in the Ready To Ride collection, there are several gender-specific pieces. 

‘The RTR women’s bibtights use a Woman Foam Bio pad,’ says Paola Santini. The Foam Bio pad offers extra cushioning for women’s sit bones and an anti-bacterial microfibre top layer is finished with seamless, zero friction edges to minimise the risk of irritation.

‘The body fabric supports the comfort of the pad because it’s a light thermal fleece,’ says Santini. ‘It’s durable, stretchy and lightly compressive, so the rider should forget they’re wearing them, but still offers lots of protection from the cold. The bibstraps extend seamlessly up from the legs using the same piece of fabric, again ensuring zero irritation in use.’

Bioracer

Him

  • Bioracer Wind Gilet, £72, buy now at bioracer.com
  • Bioracer Tempest Light Jacket, £94, buy now at bioracer.com
  • Bioracer Tempest Light Bibtights, £86, buy now at bioracer.com

If the Tempest Light Jacket looks familiar, that’s because it’s a staple of Bioracer’s winter line, though the jacket itself has been heavily changed for 2026, with the main material switching from polyester to polyamide. 

‘Polyamide feels softer and smoother against the skin while offering more stretch and flexibility. This creates a comfortable, close-to-body fit and greater freedom of movement,’ says Britt Raskin, Bioracer’s collection strategist. It also allows Bioracer to dye the fabric rather than having to print on it, so the design and colour options can be richer.

The overall remit of the jacket remains similar, though, being suitable for fast-paced, more intense riding in colder conditions or the milder months of autumn and spring due to its focus on breathability and light insulation rather than all-out weather protection.

Her

  • Bioracer Wind Gilet, £72, buy now at bioracer.com
  • Bioracer Tempest Light Jacket, £94, buy now at bioracer.com
  • Bioracer Tempest Light Bibtights, £86, buy now at bioracer.com

Bioracer’s Tempest Light Bibtights are a totally new garment. 

‘We wanted to provide something that offers the same characteristics as the Tempest Light Jacket, because winter kit that offers high breathability and comfort over bulky insulation and protection is only getting more relevant as the seasons become milder and more riders choose to ride indoors during the worst weather,’ says Raskin.

‘In comparison to the Tempest bibtights, the Tempest Light uses a lighter fabric and we’ve dropped the pixelated, reflective calf panels to prioritise breathability.’

The bibtights, like all Bioracer products, are gender-specific, so that means the use of a Vaper Women chamois that uses a structure and shape suited to the female physiology.

Pactimo

Him

  • Pactimo Vertex WX-D Jacket, £210, buy now at pactimo.com
  • Pactimo Alpine Thermal Bibtights, £152, buy now at pactimo.com

Pactimo’s Vertex WX-D jacket is designed for harsh winter conditions without being bulky or rigid thanks to the use of the brand’s Storm+ softshell laminate.

‘It’s a combination of lightweight, breathable, moisture-wicking knit fabrics bonded to either side of a high-stretch membrane,’ says Ryan White, Pactimo’s head of product. ‘It creates a soft-against-the-skin fabric that’s fully waterproof, but soft and stretchable.’

The Vertex adds insulation to the mix thanks to the inclusion of Polartec’s Alpha Direct fabric: ‘We’ve added it in select areas so the jacket can be used through winter’s harshest conditions without having to think about layering up. It’s designed to sit directly against skin or base layers with no backing fabric needed. Alpha is a low-density, high-pile knit with an open structure that transfers moisture freely while trapping your body heat.’

Her

  • Pactimo Alpine Thermal LS Jersey, £125, buy now at pactimo.com
  • Pactimo Alpine Thermal Bibtights, £152, buy now at pactimo.com

They might look understated but the Alpine Thermal bibtights have undergone extensive refinement in the tough conditions of Colorado’s Rocky Mountains.

‘The high-loft fleece we use in them provides warmth, breathability and excellent stretch,’ says White. That combination of attributes is even more impressive when it’s considered that Pactimo achieved them using recycled fabric.

‘“Can we use recycled materials?” is always our first question these days when it comes to designing kit,’ says White. ‘The nylon we use in the Alpine tights comes from fishing nets. Increasingly, recycled fabric offers the performance of virgin fabric, so it becomes a cost decision. We’re happy to take the small impact on our margin in order to use it.’

Elastic Interface’s women-specific Paris chamois sits at the heart of the Alpine tights, which also feature a zippered thigh pocket and reflective details.

entry.title: 25 Years of Epic Bikepark Leogang, Skills with Elements & Bike Festival This Weekend
entry.content:
Marking their 25th year as one of the longest-running and most popular gravity MTB destinations in Europe, we dropped in for the second time this season at The Epic Bikepark Leogang last week. It’s always a great spot to test out some of the latest mountain bike gear on killer alpine trails and the world-renowned DH track. More on those later.

But we also had a few other ulterior motives. Like a quick chance to hone some skills with the Elements Bike School instructors, and to chat with the shapers who build and maintain the trails for an upcoming Trail Tools story we have in the works.

Plus, while enjoying sunny summer weather late in the season, it was a good reminder that Bike Festival is coming to Leogang this coming weekend…

The Epic Bikepark Leogang: 25 Epic Years On

It’s kind of hard to fathom that the Leogang bikepark has been running for a quarter century. In fact, it was at another iconic European mountain bike destination where I came to this realization (and a reminder of aging and the passing of time!) Back in early March, I was testing out new tires, wheels, suspension, and (importantly) protection in Finale Ligure when I happened to end up in the same backcountry uplift as Martin Samek. The Trailwerk Wachau founder’s diploma thesis had been the impetus for the creation of the Leogang bikepark back in 2000 – a collaboration between the ski lift operator, the local town, tourism board, a local earthworks contractor, and several other supporters.

In 2001, Epic Bikepark Leogang became the first bikepark in Austria with just 4 trails – mostly catering to an elite group of expert mountain bikers. In the two and a half decades since, the big jump lines and pro-level downhill tracks are still a big focus. The park has since hosted 2x UCI MTB World Championships and 14x UCI MTB World Cup races, including DH, XC, Enduro, and even the occasional short track, 4x, dual slalom, and eliminator.

But now, we’re likely to see a much wider skill range of mountain bikers in the iconic blue gondolas – now including a healthy dose of ebikers, entry-level trail riders & kids, in addition to shredders heading for the Hot Shots jump line. Me personally, I prefer the more natural lines – call them enduro singletracks – and the classic down & dirty bikepark tracks like the recently updated Hangman I.

Bikerumor testing tracks and World Cup prototype proving ground…

In any case, Leogang lives on as an excellent spot to test new gear like the latest Maxxis DHX with its New DH casing. Or Schwalbe’s Radial casing tires before that. Then, Leatt’s ReaFlex Chest/Back Protector & X-Flow goggles before that. Or even the previous generation of Scott’s Spark XC & downcountry bikes, years earlier.

Or to just enjoy time with your family, mountain biking like I did back in my 2024 Editor’s Choice…

Or chasing pro & prototype DH bikes for more than a decade. Check out a few from my first couple of years on the ground, for good measure.

Needless to say, I’ll be returning to Leogang regularly in the future, as well.

One-On-One Training with Elements Bike School

One of the big draws for us to head to Leogang on this particular weekend was a planned Ladies Gravity Camp training day being planned by Elements Bike School, the bike trainers located just under the main lift station in the bikepark.

The idea seemed solid. Getting a group of advanced women riders together to hone their skills, hitting various natural and built-up obstacles in the bikepark to take it to the next level.

The hiccup, according to Elements, is that ever since COVID, most people coming to them to train want individual lessons, not group sessions. I asked my wife and she pretty much agreed. She’d much rather spend some one-on-one time with an instructor than worry about getting grouped with riders below her level that might keep her from progressing.

But the good news is (woman-owned) Elements still offers multiple training options for men and women. And group training is still on offer for those who want it. But they’re super flexible with individual and small group training sessions, too.

So, we went personal and met with Laura.

She focused on a few key techniques that my wife Veronika wanted to improve on… Form & on-bike positioning on passive to active drops, then working on balancing higher-speed berming techniques so left turns were as smooth as right turns.

Elements has multiple levels of both men and women coaching riders of all levels. And we came away from a relaxed 2-hour session feeling like progress was made, and there was still plenty to work on.

Elements-outdoorsports.at

Bike Festival in Leogang this weekend – October 2-4, 2026!

Now, if you want to get some bigger group riding or new bike testing on, this weekend might be your ticket.

Bike Festival Leogang kicks off this weekend at the bikepark, starting today through Sunday.

There’s a whole lot on the events calendar, including a lot of opportunities for you all to check out or test new bikes and gear in the bikepark, join in on several scheduled rides with local pros, and even get in some of your own skills training sessions with Bike Academy, too. There are lots of events for the whole family, as well. Plus, “All festival visitors will receive a 10% discount on lift tickets throughout the entire festival weekend,” so you can ride the park for even less this weekend.

Check out the full details via the Saalfelden-Leogang region tourism board site:

Saalfelden-Leogang.com

Oh, and one last thing…

25th Anniversary Photo Contest means free trail cams

Running through the end of the season until the start of November, Leogang is running a 25th anniversary photo contest via social media.

Enter to win some sick kit here – including a new Scott Gambler DH bike for one man and one woman. Plus, the side benefit is that all three of their automatic trail cameras that snap your photo as you ride past are available for free to download. You just search the time you pass each trail location – the Flying Gangster wall ride, the Flow Link hip jump, and the lower Hangman II berm.

Go ride, then download your snaps to check out your form!

Bikepark.Saalfelden-Leogang.com

entry.title: REEB and Cane Creek Announce Limited Edition STEEZL x Invert Enduro Chassis Kit
entry.content:
REEB Cycles is no stranger to limited-edition builds, and they’re at it again with Cane Creek, this time collaborating on a limited-edition STEEZL x Invert Chassis Kit. Available to order for the month of October only, this collaboration pairs the new and somewhat rare Cane Creek Invert Enduro fork with a STEEZL frame in a custom finish inspired by Cane Creek’s new Slate Chroma Studio color. 

“We didn’t want to take an Invert, bolt it onto a STEEZL and call it a collaboration,” said Jeff Lenosky, Brand Director at REEB Cycles. “Cane Creek’s new Slate color gave us the opportunity to treat the entire chassis as a one-off custom project. The dual satin/gloss powder finish, frame and fork graphics, headset, black-anodized hardware, and suspension package create this limited edition chassis and what makes this collaboration worth doing.”

Built in-house by REEB in Colorado and featuring American-made rockers, hardware, and seat clamp, the 155mm travel STEEZL frame is done up with a custom, dual-finish Lux Nightfall powder coat. That’s complemented by the Slate accents of the Cane Creek Hellbender 70 headset, black anodized  suspension hardware, and matching graphics on the frame and fork.

This limited-edition Chassis Kit is centered around Cane Creek’s new Invert Enduro fork at 170mm of travel. Officially launched back in April, the upside-down Invert Enduro fork has been highly sought after and in relatively short supply — it is currently sold out in all travel lengths. For the rear shock, buyers can choose between the Cane Creek Kitsuma Coil, Kitsuma Air, or the unique Tigon air-charged coil shock.

Chassis Kit Features

  • REEB STEEZL 155mm-travel chassis handcrafted in Colorado
  • Custom dual-finish Lux Nightfall powder coat inspired by Cane Creek Slate
  • Cane Creek Invert Enduro fork
  • Cane Creek Hellbender 70 Slate Chroma Studio headset
  • Exclusive matching REEB frame and Invert Enduro fork decal package with Slate accents
  • Black-anodized Prosise Metal Works rockers and hardware
  • Choice of Cane Creek Kitsuma Coil, Kitsuma Air, or Tigon rear shock
  • 4–6 week estimated lead time

Pricing and Availability

The limited edition STEEZL x Invert Chassis Kit starts at $5,462 and includes everything listed above. The price may increase slightly depending on the rear shock choice or the addition of ISCG tabs (+$40). Complete builds are also available, with no shortage of options in REEB’s custom build configurator. 

As mentioned above, the REEB STEEZL x Cane Creek Invert Chassis Kit is available to order for the month of October only. Head to the REEB website to learn more or place an order.

reebcycles.com

entry.title: ENVE SES 6.7 PRO Gets Hooked Rims, Higher Pressures, & $3,750 Price Tag
entry.content:
After releasing a super-rocket aerobike, ENVE has a new deep-section race wheel, and it’s already got a few wins.

The new wheelset was developed in response to the UCI rim-depth rules that took effect at the beginning of 2026. Instead of modifying the existing SES 6.7, ENVE started over with new front and rear rim shapes. They also added a new INNERDRIVE PRO hub and ceramic bearings. ENVE calls it its fastest UCI-legal wheelset to date.

The final setup pairs a 59mm front rim with a 65mm rear, just in the UCI-legal zone. The new SES 6.7 PRO (shouldn’t we be calling these the 6.5s?) weighs a claimed 1,495g with valves and tape and is built around 28mm tires.

It has also already been racing under UAE Team Emirates, with more than 10 WorldTour wins before the official launch.

New 59mm Front and 65mm Rear Rims

The SES 6.7 PRO uses different front and rear profiles, something ENVE has done throughout its SES line.

Up front is a 59mm-deep rim, while the rear grows to 65mm. Both use a 22.5mm internal width and were aerodynamically developed around a 28mm tire. ENVE says it also tested other tire sizes and at speeds representative of both professional and amateur riders. In the end, they decided the conditions and course profiles the SES PRO 6.7 would be used in were best suited to 28mm tires.

The idea behind the split depths is familiar. The front wheel has a bigger influence on steering and crosswind stability, while the rear can go deeper without affecting handling as much.

ENVE has worked with aerodynamicist Simon Smart (who also worked closely on the new ENVE Melee V2) since 2009, developing SES shapes through CFD, wind-tunnel work, in-frame testing, and outdoor riding. ENVE believes you should tune the front and rear rims separately rather than treating them as matching shapes with different depths. More companies are trending this way as well.

Built Around 28mm Tires

The 22.5mm internal width is also notable in a market where rims have continued getting wider. With 23-25mm seeming to be the default, ENVE is playing in the safer space.

Rather than chasing maximum tire volume, the focus here is matching the tire and rim shape for aerodynamics.

The SES 6.7 PRO is hookless, hooked, tubeless-only, and, like ENVE’s other premium wheelsets, built in Ogden, Utah.

INNERDRIVE PRO Saves 60 Grams

A new hub also hides between those deeper rims. The INNERDRIVE PRO is a lighter version of ENVE’s existing INNERDRIVE system and uses a redesigned 40-tooth ratchet and spring.

ENVE says the new hub saves 60 grams compared with the Premium INNERDRIVE hub.

Part of that comes from a lighter hub shell, but ENVE also reduced the ratchet diameter and removed material from the drive mechanism. A new spring uses less force while maintaining reliable engagement, reducing ratchet drag.

The hub uses ENVE PRO Ceramic Bearings with Grade 5 ceramic balls, hardened stainless-steel races, and polyamide cages. They also use low-contact seals on the outboard side to protect against dirt and water, with non-contact seals internally to reduce drag. The ceramic bearings come with a five-year factory warranty.

1,495g for a 59/65mm Wheelset

The complete wheelset weighs a claimed 1,495g, including valves and tape.

That’s a fairly respectable number given the rim depths, especially since the wheel is clearly aimed more at outright speed than gram counting. Still, its the heaviest in the ENVE SES lineup.

Already Winning at the WorldTour

Did I see this somewhere before? Yeah…we all did. The 6.7 PRO may be new to customers, but it isn’t new to racing.

ENVE says the wheelset has already collected more than 10 WorldTour victories, including Milan-San Remo, Strade Bianche, the UAE Tour, Tour of Oman, and Clásica Jaén.

UAE Team Emirates has been involved throughout the development process, using track testing to compare the new wheel against the previous version.


Hooks Are Back

One easy-to-miss detail (we originally missed it!) is the return of a hooked bead on the new SES 6.7 PRO.

The 22.5mm internal rim still requires tubeless-compatible tires, so ENVE isn’t abandoning road tubeless. But unlike the hookless SES 4.5, the 6.7 PRO uses a traditional bead hook.

Why? It raises the pressure ceiling. ENVE lists a maximum pressure of 100 psi / 7 bar for the hooked SES 6.7 PRO, compared with 72.5 psi / 5 bar for the hookless SES 4.5.

Most riders won’t need anything close to 100 psi with a 28mm tire, especially the super lightweight WorldTour riders. However, the hooked design gives the wheel more headroom and removes some of the tire-compatibility questions that continue to follow hookless road rims.

Is It Really The Fastest UCI-Legal Wheelset?

ENVE has some numbers to back up the claim. In its 48kph testing on the ENVE Melee, the SES 6.7 PRO posted the lowest drag of the conventional spoked wheelsets in the comparison. The test included the previous-generation SES 6.7, Roval Rapide CLX II, Vision Metron 60 SL, Bontrager Aeolus RSL 51, Zipp 454, Scope Artech 4, and several others.

Interestingly, the fastest conventional wheel in ENVE’s test wasn’t the deepest. The new 59/65mm SES 6.7 PRO tested faster than the outgoing 60/66mm SES 6.7. We’re betting the gains are coming from the new rim shape rather than simply adding depth.

The only setup that tested faster was ENVE’s SES 100 PRO front wheel paired with a rear disc, which is a very different setup from a normal UCI road-racing wheelset.

Tire size also played a noticeable role.

At 55kph, ENVE measured 75.3 watts of average drag with a 27.1mm tire and 75.7 watts with a 29.4mm tire. Moving up to a measured 32.3mm tire, drag increased to 78.1 watts. At 35.1mm, it jumped to 87.6 watts.

That helps explain why ENVE built the new 6.7 PRO around a 28mm tire rather than going wider.

So, is it really the fastest UCI-legal road wheelset? In ENVE’s own testing, it’s the fastest comparable spoked setup in the group they tested. Independent numbers would still be useful, but there’s at least some real data behind the claim.

ENVE SES 6.7 PRO Specs

  • Front rim depth: 59mm
  • Rear rim depth: 65mm
  • Internal rim width: 22.5mm
  • Optimized tire size: 28mm
  • Claimed weight: 1,495g including valves and tape
  • Hubs: ENVE INNERDRIVE PRO
  • Ratchet: 40-tooth PRO
  • Bearings: ENVE PRO Ceramic
  • Tire compatibility: Tubeless only
  • Manufactured in: Ogden, Utah, USA

ENVE SES 6.7 PRO Pricing

The SES 6.7 PRO is priced at:

  • USA: $3,750 complete (Front: $1,700/Rear: $2,050)
  • Europe: €4,600; UK: £4,000; Canada: $5,200 CAD

At $3,750, the SES 6.7 PRO is firmly at the top end of ENVE’s road wheel lineup.

ENVE.com

entry.title: Giant Trance & Liv Intrigue Advanced E+ eMTBs Blend Power & Traction Control
entry.content:
Giant & Liv together launch two all-new ebikes today that hope to refocus eMTB choice on not just more power, but better full-power control. Don’t worry, there’s more power too. Between 20-40% boost upgrade to 120Nm makes both the new Giant Trance Advanced E+ and Liv Intrigue Advanced E+ shoot up the climbs. And the all-new full-power eMTBs also get more travel and more capable geometry to fly downhill, as well.

But honestly, the two big upgrades in this new generation are much better control of all that pedal-assist power, and a new rider-tuned battery configuration for the women-focused Liv eMTBs.

2026 Giant Trance & Liv Intrigue Advanced E+ get more power

It feels like ever since DJI & the Avinox motor system smashed onto the ebike scene, there’s been an eMTB arms race to deliver maximum power. I think that essentially boils down to the fact that most eMTB buyers don’t get a chance to try several different powertrains before they buy. And much like range anxiety makes us pick the biggest battery possible. Power FOMO is real. And no one wants to spend a ton of money on an ebike, only to find out that it’s not powerful enough. Or worse yet, that your friend’s new ebike is more powerful, and you can’t keep up.

It’s the reason that light-assist ebikes look to be DOA, even if many of them are a lot of fun to ride.

Both the new Giant Trance Advanced E+ and Liv Intrigue Advanced E+ share the same new SyncDrive Pro 4 ebike motor developed in-house together with Yamaha. And there is certainly more pedal-assist. Significantly higher torque output, now comes to 120Nm of continuous support. And max power is up too, now at 850W peak. Plus, now with 500% max assistance, you get more eMTB motor support than ever!

No, those are not the highest figures on the eMTB market. But rest assured, that’s still a lot of power.

More controllable full power, even at zero cadence

But with greater power come greater need for control.

While it’s relatively simple to just add more peak power or higher torque, putting that into the ground through a 2.4″ wide tire on often loose terrain is a tougher challenge. And then, making a >20kg ebike manageable under full-power without shooting you off the trail, into a tree, or into shared-access traffic is a completely different story.

There’s a reason that there’s quite a lot of ongoing backlash from Avinox’s ‘more power is better‘ mindset from inside the bike industry, from trail access advocates, and even potentially from national regulators. Super power can be fun. But it also can be problematic if not well controlled.

And control is really one of the high points of the new Yamaha-produced SyncDrive Pro 4 motor at the heart of these two new Giant & Liv E+ eMTBs.

A big secret to the new motor control is its new “torque-based, zero-cadence design”. The new Giant/Liv motor claims to be able to deliver its peak torque within just 0.28 seconds of you pressing down on the pedals. And it doesn’t require the crank arms to actually move. That’s a big difference to the feel of most ebike drive systems, which require physical crank movement to match your power input.

Now with Traction Control

What that translates to is faster pedal-assist response from the Giant/Liv motor. And most importantly, the ability to restart ebike motor support almost instantly, and get moving again when you hit an obstacle and come to an unexpected stop.

Tied with more sensors in the whole system (now increased to 6), Giant/Liv add a new Traction control mode that measures power output at the chainring (plus slope and cadence) and detects slip at the rear with a wheel speed sensor. So when that bigger new power comes on too quickly and breaks the rear tire loose, the system instantly manages output up and down to make sure all of the power translates into forward motion.

The result is a lot less wheel slip than we are used to in full-power ebikes in loose conditions. And especially on really steep ascents with steps or variable traction (like loose over hardpack), the new E+ system simply puts the power down in a much more manageable way.

What about battery capacities? 840Wh or 560Wh+280Wh!

The last generation of Giant Trance Advanced E+ & Liv Intrigue Advanced E+ that we really covered in-depth, combined full power motors (85Nm & 600W, at the time) with half-size 400Wh batteries to keep weights down. In between, there was a 85Nm & 800W update with full-sized 800Wh batteries for more range.

Now, Giant and Liv separate themselves a bit to better serve the actual riders who buy their ebikes. Since the Giant’s come in larger sizes and generally get heavier riders, they come with an 840Wh removable internal battery inside the downtube.

But on the other hand, since most Liv buyers are smaller and lighter, they get a smaller, lighter 560Wh removable internal battery. But lest the Liv buyers suffer range anxiety, Liv Intrigue Advanced E+ eMTBs, at the same spec and price level as their Giant analogs, also come with an external 280Wh range extender battery. So the Liv Intrigue Advanced E+ buyers still get the same 840Wh total battery capacity, but they only have to carry the heavier setup on longer rides.

Now guys, don’t worry, you can ride further, too. The Giant Trance Advanced E+ eMTBs are also compatible with the same EnergyPak Plus range extender. It doesn’t come standard with the ebikes. But you can add on an extra 280Wh to get a max 1120Wh capacity for longer supported rides, if you buy the 280Wh range extender separately.

What else is new?

Besides the new more-powerful motor, the enhanced motor control, and the new battery options, the new Giant Trance & Liv Intrigue Advanced E+ also now get 10mm more Maestro dual-link 4-bar travel.

Both eMTBs are still mullet builds – 27.5″ rear and 29″ front wheels – but now they get 160mm front & 150mm rear travel for more technical trail capability. Because if you are hauling full-power eMTB weight around, you might as well be able to handle any trail.

Giant and Liv also reshape geometry to make these new ebikes ready for anything. Both eMTBs share the same 64.5° head angle, 77° seat angle, and 443mm chainstays.

They also both get a 3-position flip-chip at the top of the seatstays to let you go lower or higher, with a +/- 0.4° tweak to the angles.

While much is the same between the two frames, the Liv Intrigue E+ comes in 4 sizes (XS-L) with generally lower Stack and shorter Reach to fit smaller riders. And sharing the same angles, the Giant Trance E+ comes in 4 bigger sizes (S-XL).

Overall, Giant says this is the lightest full-power eMTB they’ve ever made. They saved 300g off the latest carbon frame and forged links, and dropped 1850g off total ebike weight, for a claimed total weight of 21.9kg. The Liv carbon frame is more than 100g lighter than the Giant, and the complete Intrigue Advanced E+ comes in at just 20.0kg claimed.

Interestingly, that makes this new Liv Intrigue Advanced E+ with more power and a bigger battery, just 200g heavier than the previous light model that only had a 400Wh battery inside.

Giant Trance Advanced E+ – Pricing, options & availability

The new Giant Trance Advanced E+ comes in four specs globally, all sharing the same carbon frame and SyncDrive Pro 4 ebike powertrain. The top-tier €10K Trance Advanced E+ 0 gets Fox Factory suspension, a SRAM XX AXS Transmission groupset, TRP Evo Pro brakes, and heavy-duty Giant TRX HD carbon wheels. Next, the €8000 Trance Advanced E+ 1 goes Fox Performance spec, SRAM GX AXS Transmission, and alloy Giant TRA HD wheels.

Then, the special edition €6500 Trance Advanced E+ SE gets a special ebike-tuned Crest TR Elite 36 fork and TR shock from Giant’s in-house suspension department in Taiwan, plus wireless electronic TRP drivetrain running an 11sp LinkGlide cassette with automated shifting controls. And the entry-level €6000 Trance Advanced E+ 2 goes for RockShox Psylo Gold fork, Deluxe Select shock, and a Deore mechanical 12-speed drivetrain.

Globally, the new Trance Advanced E+ eMTBs roll out to Giant dealer bike shops today. But of course, the elephant in the room is US availability. There is still a US import restriction in place, so no US availability is expected in the immediate future.

Giant-bicycles.com

Liv Intrigue Advanced E+ – Pricing, options & availability

Putting women first, to get more women on bikes, the new Liv Intrigue Advanced E+ also comes in four complete ebike builds, mostly at the same price, even with the addition of the range extender battery being included. Lighter weight for most rides was the real driver behind the smaller internal battery, to maintain control & maneuverability. But Liv thought it was important to include maximum range for those women who still want to ride further. The Liv models also include lighter shock and fork tunes, better suited for lighter riders to get the most out of their suspension, even with added ebike weight.

The flagship €10,000 Intrigue Advanced E+ 0 gets Fox Factory, SRAM XX AXS, TRP Evo Pro brakes in shiny gold, and the Giant TRX HD carbon wheels. The €8000 Intrigue Advanced E+ 1 gets Fox Performance, SRAM GX AXS, and the alloy Giant TRA HD wheels. And €6500 Intrigue Advanced E+ SE gets the Crest TR Elite 36 fork & shock, electronic TRP 11sp LinkGlide drivetrain and special edition paintjob. All three of which include the 56oWh internal battery AND the 280Wh EnergyPak Plus range extender at no extra charge, making them all great values.

The entry-level €6000 Intrigue Advanced E+ 2 does not get the range extender, but otherwise the same RockShox Psylo Gold fork, Deluxe Select shock, and Deore mechanical 12-speed spec.

Liv-cycling.com

One more thing…

A new KMC eFlat HT high-torque flattop chain!

Both new Giant & Liv E+ eMTBs also all come with a new high-torque chain that they developed together with KMC.

The new gold KMC eFlat HT was designed for SRAM Transmission derailleurs and cassettes paired to high-powered ebike powertrains, with combined rider plus motor input up to 300Nm. The new chain is said to be 21% stronger than the benchmark (read: SRAM) chain with 35% higher pin strength to prevent chain breakages on high-powered eMTB, plus significantly longer lifespan.

As someone who has broken at least 3 chains in between torque-heavy Avinox & S-Works ebikes, I really look forward to getting more time on this shiny new KMC chain!

KMCchain.com

entry.title: Elite from day one: The story behind the Italian cycling icon
entry.content:
Cyclist
Elite from day one: The story behind the Italian cycling icon

In itself, the name Elite doesn’t give much away other than a suggestion of excellence, but for the past half century the company behind it has worked hard to become one of the world’s foremost manufacturers of cycling equipment with a mission statement concise enough to fit on a bidon: make riders feel good. All this from its deep and enduring geographical roots just outside Padua, Veneto, in northeastern Italy.

Elite was founded in a garage in 1979 by Amerigo Sartore, who was working in the industry at the time and was deeply passionate about cycling. At first it was rollers and bike carriers, but fast forward a few decades and Elite’s product range today covers bidons, cages and every type of trainer for cyclists the world over, including one particularly notable rider, a certain Tadej Pogačar.

Since the turn of the century, home has been the Fornaci Serciari on a meander of the Brenta river in Fontaniva, where Elite has been working to make high-performance cycling products amidst the almost incongruous setting of 19th century brick kilns. Making things to last is in the very ground here, and it’s a suitable fit. A ten-year restoration project, completed in 2000, turned these rustic buildings – with chimneys and bricks intact – into a future-proof headquarters steeped in heritage.

Elite’s first bottle cage collections were designed inside the fornaci and named after the people of Fontaniva, further cementing the company’s link with the area. Now there are more than 120 products in the Elite catalogue, which are used by riders across the globe.

Grand Tour connections

The area of northeast Italy that Elite calls home, with its sometimes changeable mountain weather, is dripping with Grand Tour pedigree. There’s Giro stalwart Monte Grappa in the north, with its punishing 25km of ascent looming over the town of Bassano; the Pasubio, Colli Berici and Monte Berico in the west; and the volcanic Colli Euganei in the south, bursting with Classics-style 10% ramps.

In other words, Elite’s headquarters are surrounded by elite riding opportunities – this region can claim to be the most cycling-obsessed part of Italy, and with over 400 clubs and close to 10,000 licenced racers in the region you’d be brave to disagree. Grand Tours don’t route stages through Veneto just for the scenery, they come because the terrain is testing and deep crowds of passionate fans are always in attendance.

Elite through the years

Elite’s story began with a set of very simple bike rollers that formed an indoor training machine. Then came the first frame-clamped trainer in 1982, adjustable magnetic resistance in 1992 and the leap forward into digital with the first PC-connected trainer in 2000. Elite was able to put DVD race footage in front of riders in 2009 with RealAxiom while direct drive training arrived soon after in 2013. The arrival at what we recognise today as modern indoor training came in 2016 with automatic resistance control. Quite the journey.

Continuing the work of founder Amerigo Sartore is his daughter Nicoletta, who worked in almost every area of the business before taking the reins. Continuity is a key part of the ethos: a family-run, family-owned business that reinvests profits into new projects, answering to riders rather than shareholders.

Elite has been working in the WorldTour peloton since the 1990s and currently partners with more than half the world’s pro teams for technical support. That relationship is not just about brand exposure – it provides crucial feedback for Elite’s product managers and designers. 

When a rider takes a bottle at 55kmh in a crosswind on the Roubaix cobbles, the product’s design must stand up: light enough to go unnoticed, soft enough to empty in a few squeezes and secure enough not to bounce out of the bottle cage. Elite’s flagship 550ml Fly Team bottle weighs 51g. That’s after years of removing material without compromising flow or resistance. Similarly, the Leggero Carbon cage has been holding bidons for generations, and the new version sheds more grams again, making it even lighter.

Both the Fly Team and the Leggero Carbon cage are used in every WorldTour race, while Elite’s Fly Tex bottle is one of the most used bidons by cyclists worldwide. Elite is also looking to the future, with its Jet bottle made from biodegradable plastic.

Taking it indoors

Elite’s trainers are also put through their paces by the world’s best. UAE Team Emirates XRG, Groupama-FDJ United and Picnic PostNL routinely warm up and down and train using Elite’s flagship Justo 2 trainer, with several other teams using the company’s other trainers in their regimes. These riders need consistent, reliable data whether they’re in a hotel car park in August or their garage in February. Rather than fitting a third party optical torque sensor, Elite builds its own, meaning the heat generated during a workout doesn’t affect the trainer’s accuracy.

Elite’s Square smart frame lets you recreate your bike precisely, from fit position to drivetrain, ensuring your setup is consistent whether indoors or outdoors. To go alongside, Elite also produces a smart indoor fan, the Aria, to maintain optimal rider temperature.

Rolling into the future

As well as aspiring to the highest performance standards, Elite has voluntarily become a Benefit Corporation and is committed to creating value for local communities and protecting the environment. In practice, that means embedding sustainability into Elite’s products and creating designs that are built to be updatable and repairable rather than replaced; products that use less material and create less waste; packaging that’s recycled or plant-based; and manufacturing standards that are environmentally conscious.

Elite has 70 employees, some of whom have worked in Fontaniva for more than 20 years – longevity that speaks for itself. The brick kilns they work in, peering up at Monte Grappa framed by the window, have stood tall in Fontaniva for over a century. Elite is well on its way to doing exactly the same.

• To find out more about Elite’s range of products, go to elite-it.com

The post Elite from day one: The story behind the Italian cycling icon appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: Cyclist Magazine Podcast: Sir Chris Hoy
entry.content:
Cyclist
Cyclist Magazine Podcast: Sir Chris Hoy

This week on the Cyclist Magazine Podcast, James is joined by Sir Chris Hoy, who – in case you haven’t heard – was a pretty good cyclist in his day. Chris won six Olympic gold medals and one silver on the track, spanning four Olympic Games including that incredible week at the 2008 Beijing Olympics, where he won golds in the Team Sprint, Individual Sprint and Keirin as Team GB notched up a staggering 14 cycling medals, cementing Britain as a cycling powerhouse and putting cycling into the mainstream in the process.

In this episode, Chris discusses that day in Beijing as well as many other memorable moments, like sitting trackside in Athens watching world records get smashed over and over until it was his turn to compete; turning up in Japan to learn to race Keirin at Japanese Keirin school; a love of coffee that meant he never travelled anywhere without his espresso machine and grinder, and his even bigger love and respect for cycling compatriot and maverick record breaker, Graeme Obree; and which of his teammates rode with different length cranks without even noticing.

Chris also talks about his Stage 4 cancer diagnosis and how prostate cancer affects men and what men can do to catch it early. We also talk about how you can support Chris’s annual charity ride, Tour de 4, which raises money for cancer research and care, and which this year saw 191 riders with Stage 4 cancer join thousands more as they cycled and raised nearly £3 million for charity, taking Tour de 4’s total to a staggering £5.8 million in two years.

You can check your risk of prostate cancer in under 30 seconds at prostatecancer.org/risk-checker and you can donate to Tour de 4, or sign up for next year’s event at tourde4.com

Chat begins at 11:10.

  • Listen to our chat with Chris Hoy on the Cyclist magazine app or wherever you get your podcasts
  • Get the Cyclist iOS app / Get the Cyclist app on the Google Play store

This episode is brought to you by Rouvy, the indoor riding platform that makes indoor rides look and feel real, from smashing up Sa Calobra to group rides around Vietnam to Rouvy Fest, which this year takes place between 12th and 25th October and will include a host of special group rides, including tackling Mount Teide in Tenerife, riding the shores and hill of Lake Garda in Italy and puffing up dust on the Strade Bianche chalky road of Tuscany. All this plus special ride guests telling stories and answering questions as they pedal, challenges, rewards and giveaways, and the Rouvy Fest Race, a huge single race where the competitive spirit meets fun and inclusive vibes.
