entry.title: UCI World Cup Whistler DH: New and Prototype Bikes, plus Recent Products
entry.content:
As a Sea-To-Sky local for nearly 19 years, it sure was a treat to have a UCI World Cup Downhill race finally happen in Whistler, B.C.! I’ve never had the chance to attend a World Cup event, so it was great to check out the pits, the expo tents and watch the highest level of downhill racing in person. Of course, there were a few interesting bikes and products to be found at the race…

Norco had several examples of their brand new Team DH bike displayed at various locations, including team and production spec builds. Cruising around the event was an Ari 32” prototype as well, which is most likely an incoming Signal Peak XC bike. There weren’t a ton of products on display, but Lazer’s dazzling carbon and gold A-Line full-face helmet and Michelin’s everyday rider-friendly Performance Line tires caught our attention.

Norco Team DH Bikes:

Norco just launched their new Team DH downhill bike while the racers were practicing on Friday. Not surprisingly they had several bikes built up and displayed around the event grounds. In the title photo is a full production spec Team DH 2 Rockshox model, which was featured at the RideWrap expo booth. As the above photo shows, this model’s frame boasts an eye catching blue-over-silver paint job (protected with RideWrap, of course!).

Over at Norco’s tent in the pits, they were showing off a team spec build of the new DH bike. Since the team is supported by Adidas, they also teased us by displaying a pair of the new Adidas Freerider Pro BOA Clipless shoes right next to this bike. Follow the link to check out our article covering the new Freerider shoes.

Finding Greg Minnaar’s prototype Team DH bike was a nice surprise! Maxxis had the prototype Minnaar raced throughout 2024 on display at their Race Vault pop-up in Creekside Plaza.

One interesting thing about Minnaar’s bike is how Norco was wrapping the aluminum chainstays with layers of carbon fiber to experiment with different levels of stiffness. It’s always cool to see a working prototype, especially when there are production-ready builds nearby to compare it to.

Ari 32” MTB Prototype:

Just as I was leaving the race, I looked over at Fox’s booth and spotted this! No-one on hand was sharing much info on it, but it appears to be the aluminum framed Ari Signal Peak 32” XC prototype Bikerumor spotted back in April. It looks to be running the Fox 34 SL prototype fork we saw on the bike previously (this one had Fox stickers on it), and it definitely has a set of Maxxis Aspen tires. The dropped stem on this bike bore the word ‘PROTOTYPE’ on its side.

It sounded like this bike was quickly assembled as a showpiece, as someone in the booth mentioned there may not be fluid in the brake lines. Ari’s website currently has a teaser page for the incoming 32” bike, where you can sign up to get news updates.  

Lazer A-Line KinetiCore Full-Face Helmet:

On display at Shimano’s booth was this awesome looking A-Line KinetiCore full-face helmet from Lazer. I’ve always liked bare carbon patterns, but I’ve never seen anyone incorporate gold into the carbon like this! The gold gilded backside of this helmet looked amazing as the sun bounced off it.

The Lazer A-Line KinetiCore helmet was announced back in July, but retail stores just recently received their first shipments.  

Michelin Performance Line MTB and eMTB Tires:

Michelin was showing their line of Wild Enduro MTB and E-Wild eMTB tires in Whistler. The grippy single compound Racing models of these tires have been available for a while, but at the beginning of this year Michelin introduced the Performance Line models. These newer versions are aimed at recreational riders who want a longer lasting tread, rather than a super soft race day tire.

The Performance Line tires feature the exact same tread patterns as the equivalent Racing models. They utilize a dual compound design, with firmer rubber in the middle and Michelin’s racing compound rubber on the sides. This offers longer wear and faster rolling speed versus the Racing tires. The Performance Line tires also feature more compliant sidewalls than the Racing models, and weigh in a little lighter. Shown in Whistler were the Performance Line E-Wild front and rear tires, and the Wild Enduro MS and MH models.

entry.title: Sneak Peek: Unreleased Avona 32″ Carbon Callis Gravel Bike Wins UCI World Series Race
entry.content:
Big wheels keep on rolling, and those 32″ wheels keep winning races. Back at Sea Otter Europe in Girona, we got a good look at the unreleased 32″ carbon Avona Callis gravel bike that Leon Kaiser raced for the win at the UCI World Series Race in Girona. And thanks to Avona’s liberal teasing of the bike at the show, we also now know that the bike will be available to consumers in just two weeks.

That likely makes this the first production carbon gravel race bike on 32″ wheels that you will be able to ride out of a bike shop this month!

Avona Callis 32″ carbon gravel race bike, coming soon!

Avona’s upcoming 32″ gravel bike looks a lot like the 700c carbon Callis gravel race bike that we test-rode last year. And it likely follows much of the same ethos – a premium race-ready gravel bike that blends light weight with aerodynamic nods, quick handling, tidy integration, and high-performance component spec in even the small details. All combined in the original Callis, it made for a pretty killer fast gravel all-rounder.

And clearly, this new 32″ iteration is built to go fast.

The UCI World Series Race in Girona on September 19th was a relatively short one in the gravel racing world, at just 109km with 980m of elevation to tackle. And it was reasonably quick at just over 3 hours, with more than 35km/hr average speed. An interesting aspect of the race, XC mountain biker Kaiser’s victory on the bigger wheels came in a 3-up sprint at the finish.

One of the theoretical downsides of going with larger diameter 32″ wheels is the additional work to accelerate bigger wheels with heavier rims & tires. But that clearly didn’t hold Leon Kaiser back!

Tech details

What we know about his race-winning 32″ Avona Callis gravel bike is that it shares many of the same details as its 700c predecessor.

It again gets plenty of aero integration details. From the fully integrated internal cable routing through the 1-piece Faserwerk cockpit to its smooth fork crown transition into the downtube. Frame tubing shapes are still quite small. But Avona manages to fit the same internal frame storage into the downtube under the cage mount.

Frame shaping necessitates a more-sloping toptube to ensure standover with the big 32″ wheels. But there still appears to be plenty of room inside the main triangle for two full-size water bottles, both on Kaiser’s size L frame, and a smaller M we saw in the Avona tent.

The new 32″ bike gets a UDH to fit all the most modern gravel drivetrains, but looks to be 1x and electronic only. Kaiser opted for an XTR Di2 derailleur and cassette setup, pairing a 42-tooth GRX crankset to a 10-51T cassette out back.

The 32″ Callis gravel bike also looks to get a threaded bottom bracket, and the same D-shaped aero seatpost with a hidden wedge clamp like the 700c Callis. Like most 32″ gravel bikes though, this one does appear to use Boost MTB spacing – 110x15mm up front & 148x12mm out back.

Prototype 32″ Newmen Streem G.62 CS aero carbon-spoked wheels

Also noteworthy, this race-winning 32″ Avona Callis bike was sporting some also-unreleased 32″ Newmen Streem G.62 CS deep aero carbon wheels with aero-bladed Vonoa carbon spokes.

They look pretty much exactly the same as the 700c G.62s that launched midsummer, just now in a larger diameter. Avona suggested that the carbon-spoked Newmen wheels offered a significant stiffness boost over steel spokes, making them an ideal choice for fast gravel racing on the bigger wheels. But perhaps, everyday 32″ gravel riders would prefer the bit more comfort you would get from conventional steel-spoked wheels.

Kaiser raced on prototype 32″ Newmen wheels with their flashy Pro-style silver decals. But Avona also had more subtle black-on-raw carbon decals on their own 32″ Callis gravel preview bikes, suggesting they will be a regular option at launch in a couple of weeks.

32″ Avona Callis gravel bike – Options & availability

At Sea Otter Europe, we saw 32″ Callis frames marked as sizes Medium and Large. All were built up with SRAM Force AXS Xplr groupsets. And with either these new Newmen carbon-spoke wheels, or more conventional-looking carbon wheels under Avona’s own Faserwerk branding.

Avona didn’t appear to have any bikes labeled smaller than medium. But this purple M looked pretty small. And with the spacers under the stem removed and the same zero-offset seatpost they already offer on their 700c Callis, Avona could likely fit pretty small riders on these big wheels.

Regarding when you can get your own, Avona says the bike will be available from the 15th of October through their dealer network. We will have full pricing, more detailed model specs, and even first ride impressions on the new race-winning 32″ gravel bike then!

Avona.cc

entry.title: Granite Stash RT Ratchet is my Favorite On-Bike Multitool
entry.content:
If I had to design the ultimate hidden tool to go on the bike, it would probably end up looking just like the Granite Stash RT. This compact unit sits inside the steerer tube, has a two-way ratchet with all the right bits, and stays perfectly secure and out of sight until needed.

In fact, I like this so much, I’ve put one on several of my and my family members’ mountain bikes. You should to, and here’s why…

1. It Does Everything

One of the biggest challenges with normal multi tools that fold open is trying to adjust saddle angle. Most posts’ dual bolts on the head aren’t as tool-friendly as the Fox Transfer with an angled bolt, but even this one is difficult with a bulky mini-tool. But a tiny ratchet and bit? Easy peasy.

And it works everywhere else on the bike, too:

That includes pedals, thru axles, seatpost clamps, cockpit bits, brake rotor bolts, and more.

It even makes bottle cage installation and removal super easy, because bits can insert into the end of the handle, too. I put the 8mm bit into the ratchet part to serve as a little handle for more leverage, and use the long, thin handle to reach between the curves of a bottle cage!

2. It Has Everything You Need…

…as long as you don’t need a flat head screwdriver. But it has a Phillips Head with an extended length. The Ratchet nests into the backside of the sleeve, and all of the bits are held in place magnetically. So, they’re easy enough to remove even with full finger gloves, but secure enough to stay in place during handling.

3. It’s Super Easy to Access

Even if you’re using the Hammerhead Karoo computer mount, which protrudes rearward over the steerer using the K-Edge mount as shown, it’s easy to access the tool. Just swivel the cap out of the way and the Stash RT pops up from a spring-loaded base.

Granite also makes a replacement cap with a Wahoo/Garmin-compatible computer mount, so you can combine all the things into a single unit.

4. It’s Easy to Install

The Stash RT only fits inside tapered suspension forks with an open steerer, which is a shame because I’d love to have this on my road and gravel bikes, too. But for MTB, it’s an incredibly easy install. Just choose the right length bolt from the three included, drop it into the sleeve, and thread it into the base that covers the hole on the bottom of your fork:

You can’t tell from these photos, but there’s a tall sleeve on the lower “nut”, giving you a lot of thread depth for a secure mount. This replaces the star nut, so you’ll need to pound that out through the bottom of your steerer tube to install this. Or just buy a new fork.

5. It’s Lightweight

The entire system is just 158g (with mid-length bolt). That’s about the weight of a comparable folding mini tool on its own, but you can’t hide that on your frame and still have it instantly accessible.

I have a lot of different brands’ mini tools on various bikes, including several that mount inside the steerer tube. But none are as quick and easy to use as the Stash RT. For road and gravel (or just any carbon fork without an opening at the bottom), Granite makes a version with a standard mini-tool that has tiny fold-out bits, and it’s fine, but it’s nowhere near as easy to use IRL. Still good, but if you’ve got a suspension fork, the Stash RT is the best mini-tool you can put in there.

Granite-Design.com

entry.title: ‘I only have admiration for Pogačar. I think he can beat more of my records’: Eddy Merckx interview
entry.content:
Cyclist
‘I only have admiration for Pogačar. I think he can beat more of my records’: Eddy Merckx interview

Cyclist: Fifty years have passed since your last race victory, yet you still hold the record for the most race wins in a pro career. How many of those races do you actually remember?

Eddy Merckx: I remember a lot of races, but not all 525 wins, of course. I do remember the most important ones. My first Tour de France, for example. My first Milan-San Remo in 1966, Paris-Roubaix in 1968, my Hour record…

That’s pretty good going. Do you ever think about how those races played out?

No. I try to remember those races I did in the past, but it’s not something I look back on every day. I don’t live in the past. I’m watching the current racing, not thinking about the old.

Is there anything you regret in your career? Any races you wish you had added to your palmarès?

The only thing I regret is the crash I had at the 1975 Tour de France. I suffered a double fracture to my jawbone, and that cut my career short.

I never won Paris-Tours, but I don’t miss that. I reckon I’ve won enough races to be satisfied with what I’ve achieved.

You’ve previously cited your Tour de France victory in 1969 as a career highlight. Are there any other wins you look back on with real pride?

Of course, the Hour record – 25th October 1972. I don’t remember all the dates but I remember that one. I should mention the World Championships too. The first Tour de France with the rainbow jersey on my shoulders felt very special.

Given the sheer number of races you won in your career, did you ever get bored with winning?

The opposite. It never bored me. Instead it motivated me to try and win more. You see, I did something I loved as a job, and what I loved was winning. So for me, when I went to a race, it was to win. I wasn’t there to just take part. That’s why I loved what I did back then. It still gives me pleasure to know that riders see me as the man who inspired them to win races.

These days riders are signing contracts worth millions of euros per year. Do you ever feel hard done by that you never got the same financial reward in your time?

We don’t do sport for the money. Not at all. We do it for passion. They earn much more today than I did, but I probably earned more than the riders before me. These things change with time and I don’t have any envy about that. Money is not the motivating factor for us to get into sports. 

Let’s say you were 20 years old right now. Would you want to be a pro rider in the current generation?

Absolutely, but I’d like to race more than today’s riders. I enjoyed racing, but these current pros seem to be doing it less and less.

What type of rider do you think you’d be in the modern peloton?

I think I’d be both a stage racer and a one-day rider – a complete rider like Tadej Pogačar. I don’t know if I would be stronger or weaker than him, but that’s the type of rider I think I’m closest to.

Pogačar has been touted as the next man to take over your role as cycling’s GOAT – greatest of all time. Do you think he’s similar to you at all?

I think he’s got the same ambition. When he goes to a race, he’s there to win it. He’s like me in that sense – he’s not just there to show up.

He’s a complete rider but the eras are different. We can’t compare Tadej Pogačar and Eddy Merckx; it’s different now from what it was in my day.

Do you think you could have beaten Pogačar in your prime?

Ah, the question arises. I don’t know if I could, but I’d try. I’d maybe beat him in a time-trial, but I’m not sure if I could climb as well as him these days.

You can’t compare yesterday with today. Everything is different: the nutrition, the management, the kit.

Do you feel challenged when Pogačar breaks one of your long-standing records?

The opposite. I only have admiration for Pogačar. It gives me lots of satisfaction to see him riding up the climbs with such ease. I’m sure Pogačar can beat Mark Cavendish’s stage-winning record. I think he can beat more of my records. They’re meant to be broken, so the time will come.

Which riders in the current peloton excite you the most?

Pogačar, of course. Mathieu van der Poel is a super champion and so is Wout van Aert. I like Jonathan Milan, Jasper Philipsen, Evenepoel of course, and Vingegaard.

I like it when these big riders do the one-day races – Milan-San Remo, Tour of Flanders, Paris-Roubaix – then the Grand Tours. I used to race 195 days a year. Nowadays the riders can only do 80 race days per year. I just wish they’d compete more often.

It has been 50 years since a Belgian last won the Tour de France. Do you think Belgium will have to wait long for another Tour de France champion?

At the moment there’s nobody. Evenepoel can beat Pogačar against the clock, but he can’t in a full Tour de France.

Maybe in the future Belgium will have a rider like [France’s] Paul Seixas, who has the real qualities to improve in the years to come. We’ve already seen he can come close to Pogačar, but currently there’s just not a rider like Seixas for us to win the Tour de France.

Do you consider yourself a legend?

Yes I think I’m a legend. When I look at the number of races I won during my career, it’s exceptional. I’m not just someone from my era – I’m known around the cycling community. Breitling wouldn’t have made a watch for me if I wasn’t a legend.

The post ‘I only have admiration for Pogačar. I think he can beat more of my records’: Eddy Merckx interview appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: 1Up USA Recon Rack and RakAttach: A Long Term Review – Paul Kalifatidi
entry.content:
1Up USA makes all of its bike racks in Dickeyville, Wisconsin, including its vertical carry Recon Rack. These racks and accessories are known for superior build quality, durability, and repairability, so it’s not often that they need to update their designs. In 2024, 1Up released an update to the Recon Rack, a vertical carry rack designed to haul several bikes. For the past year, Paul has been using one in combination with the RakAttach hitch receiver swing-out. Follow along for his review of the mk. 2 Recon Rack and mk.3 RakAttach from 1Up USA.

The vertical carry rack is a mainstay in my home in Bellingham, WA. We have a ton of families that ride bikes and regularly need to carry four or more bicycles. Lots of people also have them just to cut down on the number of cars needed to get everyone and their bikes to the trailhead. If there’s anything all cyclists can agree on, it’s fewer cars on the road.

I have been using the 1Up USA Recon Rack mk.2 in conjunction with their RakAttach mk.3 swing-out receiver since last August. Like all of their products, I have mostly great things to say, with a few caveats. Follow along for my review.

1Up Recon Rack mk. 2 Quick Hits

  • Full bolt-together design
  • Blend of aluminum and steel components for a high strength-to-weight ratio
  • Pivoting design makes for easy loading
  • Off-road rated with included stability straps
  • Anti-wobble design eliminates play between the rack and receiver
  • Clearance for 24” to 32” wheels, up to 5” wide, max 56″ wheelbase
  • Available in 4, 5, and 6 bike configurations
  • Rack weight:
    • Recon 4: 72 lbs
    • Recon 5: 80 lbs
    • Recon 6: 87 lbs
  • Carrying capacity: 45 lbs per basket
  • 2″ receiver only
  • Compatible with APS panel accessories
  • Made in WI, USA with lifetime warranty

I Like Bike Racks

I like cars. That’s a crazy start to an article in this publication, I know – let me explain. I like the tool that is a car; being able to transport myself, many of my friends, belongings, and hobbies across great distances while simultaneously getting to know a machine that feels more alive than just a lump of metal is a wonderful hobby. It’s why I write Radical Rigs, a series supported by 1Up USA.

Even though I love cars, I rarely drive. In my day-to-day life, I tend to drive my car maybe once a week. I hate cars and how much of our world we’ve handed over to parking lots, pedestrian-unfriendly infrastructure, and the isolating convenience of metal cages. This is a complex issue, but I love a classic American road trip with bikes. We live in a beautiful world. I think the bike rack helps us see more of it.

I don’t have time or energy for janky bike racks made of plastic parts and poor design, so I’ve always been drawn to 1Up USA’s durable and utilitarian design. Let’s get into my review.

1Up Recon Rack Assembly

The Recon Rack arrives in a few boxes. Assembly took me about an hour and was fairly straightforward. I thought I could do it on intuition, but my advice is to set ego aside and simply follow the instructions. They just work.

If you can work on bikes, you can assemble this rack. One issue with the Recon Rack’s easily assembled, repairable design is the number of fasteners that can vibrate loose. The Recon 4 has many bolts. While I have yet to find any that have shaken themselves free, I have found two that became finger-tight loose over time.

Since going through a second time and giving all of the bolts and nylock nuts a second torque, I have had no issues. I have gotten into the habit of occasionally checking them when I have my socket wrench on hand during other car maintenance duties. I don’t think this is a bad design, as I’d much prefer being able to rebuild something with nuts and bolts rather than a torch and a welder.

1Up Recon Durability, Repairability, and Build Quality

The repairability and the durability of any piece of equipment are perhaps the most important criteria I consider when choosing a product. This is why I have always been drawn to 1Up’s racks. Their platform racks are the most durable on the market. I have seen the plastic parts on other brands’ racks slowly disintegrate, while 1Up’s fading anodized finish seems to be the only sign of age. Not only are their platform racks long-lasting, but they are repairable with simple tools and an easy-to-use spare parts catalog. I have even Frankensteined a hitch rack out of their roof rack just using their part diagrams.

The rack is burly, as expected for off-road-rated equipment. It is constructed out of a blend of steel and aluminum. The stinger, upright, and horizontal beams are made of steel as they carry the bulk of the load. The baskets and various other brackets are made of aluminum. This saves a considerable amount of weight compared to the previous design. The entire system is anchored into the hitch receiver using a very secure anti-wobble design. A wedge expands inside the receiver to eliminate all play in the system. It works well and creates a stiff platform.

Off-Road Use

1Up supplies two cam straps for off-road use. These tension the top of the rack to the hitch receiver and create a more rigid system. There is noticeably less movement when using the straps. When driving off-road with a bike rack, the biggest issue is dragging the rack over obstacles while the vehicle undulates across an uneven surface. The Recon Rack’s skeleton is a 90-degree bend from the stinger (which enters the hitch receiver) and the upright (which holds the bikes). This rack sticks quite far out of the back of my truck, further accentuated by my use of the RakAttach swingout.

The combination of swingout and long stinger results in a lesser departure angle (the measure of how steep an incline the vehicle can navigate before putting the rack into the ground). I have scraped and banged the rack many times, mostly when crossing small creeks and depressions. Some other vertical racks mitigate this issue by using two 45-degree bends as opposed to one 90-degree bend. That said, the rack is durable, and I haven’t damaged it beyond scratches and gouges.

Loading Bikes

Loading bikes is simple if you are tall and on a level surface. I’m 5’10” and don’t have an issue lifting 35-pound bikes into the baskets. My 5’4″ friend was able to load bikes without lowering the rack, but it wasn’t the easiest for her. If you are shorter or less able, then this might be a challenge, and I recommend lowering the rack halfway. It is easiest to load bikes right to left, like reading, and to remove in the opposite direction. I occasionally ran into the issue of handlebars and top tubes interfering with one another. Unlike the platform racks from 1Up, there isn’t any way to adjust the bikes’ position in relation to one another, so you have to rearrange the order of bikes to make clearance.

Securing Bikes

Once situated, the front wheel rests in the basket and the rear wheel leans into the lower crossbar. Most vertical racks secure bikes at the top of the rack in a basket or by holding the wheel, stem, or fork crown with a strap. There is no strap at the top of the Recon Rack; 1 Up approaches this completely differently. There is a cam strap that goes around the pedal spindle, around a hook, through the rear wheel, and to another hook on the crossbar. This single strap pulls the bike down into the basket and against the lower crossbar. It is quite effective, but I do have my issues with it.

The problem with this system is that the strap can trap slack. While parts of the system might be tight, there could be strapped layers of slack. Once moving, this slack can work itself into the whole system. The result could be catastrophic if the strap manages to jump out of one of the wheel hooks or off the pedal. I found the best way to take up slack in the cam strap is to put the strapped pedal at 6 o’clock and then move it through the pedal stroke. Then I jostle and adjust until I can confirm that there isn’t any slack left to remove. It requires some mindfulness.

These straps are fully removable, meaning that they do not face the elements when not in use. It does mean that they are more easily misplaced, and indeed, I somehow lost two of them. You can order straps from 1Up, but you can also use generic cam straps found at any hardware or outdoor store. I cut some NRS straps that I already had to the proper length and used those.

Recon Rack Bike Compatibility

1Up USA states that the rack is compatible with 24” to 29” wheels up to 5″ wide and wheelbases up to 54″ long. 1Up also sells a kit that adapts the rack to children’s bikes with wheels smaller than 24″. I also have a 32″ bike in for review and it fits just fine in the wheel basket, although 1Up has yet to come out and say that this wheel size is supported by the Recon Rack. They did release a kit that makes their other racks compatible with 32″ wheels, but the Recon has yet to see any official upgrade kit. I suspect that it does not need one. When loading road bikes or gravel bikes, take care not to smack the downtube on the wheel basket.

Tilting the Recon Rack

The mechanism for tilting the rack down requires more fiddling than I feel like it should. There is a pin that locks the rack in the upright position and a lever that actuates a stopper in the hinge. With cold or muddy hands, I have bashed my knuckles while inserting or removing the cotter pin through the hinge. Some play in the sandwiched steel pieces and plastic bushing of the hinge assembly makes it challenging to line up all the holes for the pin. I end up pushing the rack back and forth while wiggling the pin to remove or insert it. This isn’t very challenging when the rack is empty, but when bikes are loaded, it’s far harder.

If you want to lower it all the way down, then there is a second pin that needs to be removed. I rarely messed with that second pin. The rack doesn’t hinge all the way to the ground, and you can’t load bikes with that pin removed, so I don’t quite understand the point. Frankly, the entire tilting mechanism became unnecessary for me, given the use of the swingout and my ability as a 5’10” human to load bikes in the vertical position. So keep that in mind.

Noises

Lastly, I ran into some noises. The most annoying was the intermittent metallic rattle that seemed to come from the latching mechanism actuated by the red lever on the upright portion of the rack. I got rid of it by putting a piece of electrical tape over that lever to dampen things. It works, but it does get in the way of tilting the rack.

There was some pretty severe squealing from the joint after some dusty road tripping. It sounded like a dying dinosaur. I learned the hard way not to add lubricant to the system, as that turned my dying dinosaur into a zombie dinosaur. A neighbor even walked over and asked if I wanted WD-40. I informed him that lubricant only angers the beast. I then proceeded to dismantle the hinge and thoroughly clean it. This vanquished the dinosaur noise. So if it starts to sound like Jurassic Park, don’t lubricate it; just clean it. You don’t even have to do a full disassembly; just move things around with water spraying into the joints.

Pros

  • Easily and securely carries 1-6 bikes, depending on the model you choose
  • Relatively easy to load and unload
  • User-rebuildable design makes replacing damaged parts easy
  • No plastic or fabric left to rot in the elements
  • Rated for off-road use
  • Anti-wobble mechanism works great
  • Compatible with APS panel accessories

Cons

  • Strap system increases odds of human error
  • Lowering rack is quite fiddly with multiple pins and slight tolerance issues
  • Can rattle
  • Severe hang-over makes for poor departure angle

See the Recon Rack at 1Up USA.

1Up RakAttach mk. 3

The 1Up RakAttach name has been in use for a while; 1Up is now on the third generation of their standard swing-out hitch receiver. I have had it for more than a year now and have found all of the parts that shine and those that could be better. And though I don’t think it is 1Up’s finest product, it has been on my truck for over a year without issue.

Quick Hits

  • Swingout Weight: 56 lbs
  • Total Weight Capacity: 275 lbs
  • Receiver Size: 2″
  • Swings out 100 degrees
  • Offroad rated
  • Material: Powder-coated steel
  • Includes Anti-Wobble Bracket and locking hitch pin
  • Compatible with various accessories like APS panel, table, and roof rack adapter bracket
  • Cannot be used for towing

Why a Swingout?

Mostly: practicality. If you have a car like my KZJ95 Prado that has a side-opening trunk, accessing the rear of the vehicle with bikes on a rack is basically a non-starter. Without a swingout, I am constantly holding my trunk to make sure it doesn’t hit my bike rack while shimmying whatever object I’m trying to place or retrieve through the cracked door. Tilting the laden bike rack down won’t drastically change that amount of space I have to work with. On vehicles like Subarus where the trunk opens up, you’ll likely find greater success in getting your trunk fully open, but you still have to dodge handlebars and tires to actually have access to the trunk space. Even with one bike on a rack, tilting it becomes a bit of a cumbersome task. Many? I hope you’re warmed up for your best hang-clean.

Easily the biggest selling point of a swing-out is the unencumbered access to the rear of the vehicle. No longer are you snagging yourself on handlebars or bashing knees on platforms. Truly, it makes the headaches of a bike rack mostly disappear. Additionally, if you are sleeping in your vehicle while camping, it creates a safe, lockable spot for your bikes where they are not in the way of meal prep and aren’t spending a night locked up to a hedge. They are secure, yet out of the way.

What I Like About the RakAttach

The all-steel construction, heavy-duty hardware, and simplicity are confidence-inspiring. 1Up states that this swing-out is off-road rated, and I believe them. It’s built like a tank. I don’t drive like a Hoonigan off-road, but I do bash my rack on rocks every now and then. The RakAttach has held up fine.

It has a weight rating of 275 pounds. Let’s assume you’re loading 35-pound bikes on 1Up’s 47-pound Heavy Duty two-tray platform with two of the add-on platforms for a capacity of four bikes. You’d only be loading the RakAttach with 224 pounds. Impressive. I have the vertical-carry Recon Rack, four-bike capacity, currently mounted. In total, four enduro bikes and the rack add up to 252 pounds; still safe. I don’t need more capacity; I don’t carry any bikes heavier than ~40 pounds and can’t fit more than five riders in my car anyways. So, this system works great for me.

There also isn’t a ton to maintain on this swingout, as one would hope for a piece of hardware that spends its time in the wheel spray of a vehicle. Instead of swiveling on a large and expensive ball bearing, it uses a durable set of bushings that are less likely to develop play and more easily serviceable. After particularly dusty miles, there is a bit of added friction, but this is quickly alleviated with a rinse of water. DO NOT use a lubricant. As with the Recon Rack, lubricant angers the dusty beast. The bushings are not designed with a lubricant in mind, and adding one will further increase the accumulation of contaminants. Overall, this swing-out is durable and reliable.

Underbaked Anti-Wobble

The most obvious and frustrating aspect of the RakAttach is the underbaked anti-wobble mechanism that seems completely out of place on a 1Up product. In most of their products, there is a wedge or ball that forces the stinger into a corner of the receiver, where it won’t move, wobble, or sag. On the RakAttach, there is no such thing.

Instead, the hitch pin is a bolt that threads into a bracket on the inside of the stinger. The goal is to suck the stinger to the side of the receiver, eliminating wobble. In a perfect world, this would work. The issue is that the hitch receiver on my Prado has a weld relatively close to the hitchpin hole. This meant that I had to trim the washer of the hitchpin bolt to clear the weld. Still, this bolt gradually loosened over time and introduced play into the system. There is nothing indexing the stinger in the vertical axis, only the horizontal. I know I’m not alone in this, as I’ve read other reports and reviews stating the same thing: occasionally tightening that bolt is necessary.

I would happily pay a bit more money if 1Up could incorporate the same anti-wobble mechanism in the RakAttach that is in the Recon Rack. I did ask 1Up if that would ever happen, and they responded with a bit of insight into why this system is as it is. The current insert and hitchpin bolt works in any orientation. This is the key to making the flippable design work and allows you to choose the direction in which the RakAttach opens.

Recently, 1Up USA announced the RakAttach XL, an even burlier swingout with a higher carrying capacity of 375 pounds and a much better anti-wobble design similar to the one on the Recon rack. I don’t need a swingout that weighs ~20 pounds more and has a higher weight capacity, but if you do, the XL is going to be a great option.

Operating the Swingout

Most swingouts have redundant systems to prevent catastrophe. On the RakAttach, this is a magnetic pin in the joint that acts as a stopper if the clamping mechanism at the swingout’s center fails. The clamp is the main closure that eliminates play in the system; the pin is the redundancy. The pin also acts as a stopper when the rack is open; there are two holes allowing you to choose half-open or fully-open positions. I added some tic marks with a gold Sharpie so it was easier to see the positions in which the hole align. Was it necessary? No, but I do think it is an easy and free upgrade.

The issue I have with the clamp and pin arrangement is in accessing both of them. If you have a bike on the rack, or something else in the way, like a spare tire and Colfax Design Works QR tire bag, you might still have to walk around to both sides to remove the pin, then undo the clamp. Otherwise you get stuck in this awkward position of trying to manipulate them from a single side while crawling under whatever obstruction is in the way. I did eventually get used to the workflow. It’s a small concession for such flexibility.

Another minor issue is that this pin is magnetic, and accumulates magnetic debris or traps sand underneath it. This has worn away at the powdercoat and resulted in small amounts of rust. It’s nothing a little bit of cleaning and paint can’t fix, but still, it feels like a slightly overengineered solution that introduced a new issue. That is generally how I feel about putting magnets in strange places.

RakAttach Accessories

The RakAttach offers some optional add-on features. I purchased the traction bar upgrade that bolts to the top of the swing-out to offer a bit more purchase in wet or muddy conditions. It’s great for crawling onto my bed platform or accessing the top of my car for cleaning or roof-mounted accessories. It’s a more durable solution than grip tape, but admittedly more expensive. Another optional accessory would be 1Up’s APS MOLLE panel, which adds options for any MOLLE-compatible gear that you might want to carry (like jerry cans, traction boards, etc). Most interesting, at least to me, would be adding the folding table upgrade to this system. There is also a bracket that you can add to adapt a 1Up roof rack to the swingout, if you have a roof rack and want to increase the total bike holding capacity of this system.

TL;DR

Long story short: I like this product, even with its downsides. It’s not perfect, but it works. It gets the bike rack out of the way while being burly and adaptable. The anti-wobble mechanism needs attention once in a while, but this is because the swingout can be flipped in either direction. This is a great swingout if your hitch receiver has ample clearance around the hitchpin hole and you need to carry up to 275 pounds of gear/bikes.

Pros

  • Super burly design is confidence-inspiring
  • Designed to open in either direction
  • Compatible with APS MOLLE panel accessories
  • Weight capacity of 275 pounds
  • Offroad rated

Cons

  • Anti-wobble mechanism does not work well
  • Design requires access to both ends of the rack
  • Magnetic pin accumulates debris and damages powdercoat

See the RakAttach at 1Up USA.

The post 1Up USA Recon Rack and RakAttach: A Long Term Review appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: More Wild Horses Than Cars
entry.content:
Thirty riders, eighty-eight miles, and the quiet fall backcountry of Routt County. Rapha x Moots Brevet, a fall gravel ride out of Steamboat Springs, Colorado.

Words by Richard Jara · Photos by Keegan Ashton, Nate Bradley


Friday

The factory is winding down on a Friday evening. The welding torches are off, and tubing sits racked along the walls in the miter shop. Evening light shines through settling into the corners. On the Friday before the Brevet, the shop floor filled with riders who had driven in, most of them from Boulder and the Front Range. We started the night with a tour, a look into the process behind a handbuilt titanium gravel bike, and a look back at Moots' history as we celebrate our 45th anniversary. Then we shared food and drinks to fuel up for Saturday's ride.

A brevet isn't a race. No clock, no podium, no free socks. There's the route, the people on it with you, and the experience shared after a hard day.

This day asked a lot.

Saturday morning. Thirty riders gather outside the Moots factory for the start.


The Climb

Wolf Mountain to Sand Mountain. The loop strings together some of our favorite roads and surfaces, from champagne gravel to rocky, rooted two-track over the divide.

The Route · 87.6 mi · 8,416 ft of climbing

Ride it yourself: Wolf Mountain x Sand Mountain on Ride with GPS →

The loop leaves the valley quickly, turning onto dirt county roads and winding through Mystic to the base of Wolf Mountain. If you weren't committed to the full route this was your chance to cut the route shorter. Long fence lines, grazing cows, and the quiet chill of morning. Golden, sunburnt hills in every direction, with dark pines along the high ridges, and off to the north sits the watershed divide we'd be crossing hours later. Recent rains had packed the dirt firm. We couldn't have asked for a better window.

More wild horses than cars. Somewhere in California Park, Routt National Forest

The climbing doesn't let up. It builds steadily through the first half, mile after mile, until the high point near mile fifty. By then the group had strung out across the route.

Nate Bradley putting the new Routt through its paces. Meet the new Routt →


Sand Mountain

The descent off Sand Mountain was, in Torin Lackmann's words, "chonky" loose, rocky, and a little above everyone's comfort zone. At the bottom, a pop-up aid station was waiting. Huge thanks to Gina, Keegan, and Indy for being there with food, water, and good spirits for a lot of tired souls.

Food, water, and good spirits at the bottom of Sand Mountain.


Home

From there, thirty miles and about 2,000 feet of climbing stood between us and the finish, most of it trending downhill. After Sand Mountain, the final stretch felt well earned, smooth champagne gravel over long, rolling hills, with the valley and Steamboat slowly coming back into view.

"The absolute fall ride of my dreams. Has to be my favorite single day out of the year. So pretty. So fun. So flowy. All. Time."

— Torin Lackmann, Rapha Boulder

Thirty riders rolled out that morning. They rolled back in dusty, cooked, and grinning. Post-ride beers waiting.

"Although there were a couple of hard, dark moments, everyone seemed to have an amazing ride. One rider told us back at the shop that afternoon it was the best gravel ride he'd ever done, hands down. We're truly lucky to have terrain like this right outside our front door. It validates why we make the bikes we do."

— Nate Bradley, Moots

We build bikes like the new Routt for days like this. Long days, rough roads, and every side of the map to explore.

Thanks to Rapha Boulder for making the trip to our corner of Colorado and making the roads we know by heart feel new again, and to all thirty of you for riding them with us.

Want to ride it yourself? Here's the route.

See you out there.

entry.title: UEC European Road Championships 2026 preview: Routes, favourites and how to watch
entry.content:
Cyclist
UEC European Road Championships 2026 preview: Routes, favourites and how to watch

The 2026 UEC European Championships will take place from Friday 2nd to Wednesday 7th October 2026 in Ljubljana, Slovenia, not even a week after the World Championships. It reverses the programme from Montreal, kicking things off with the road races and ending with a full day dedicated to all the individual time-trials.

The course is hilly, with the circuit used across the races repeating the Možjanca climb, which features gradients up to almost 16% – perfect for Slovenian native Tadej Pogačar, if he hadn’t ended his season early.

Last year, the elite road races were won by Pogačar and Demi Vollering with time-trial victories going to Remco Evenepoel and Marlen Reusser. The U23 road races were won by Jarno Widar and Paula Blasim while Jonathan Vervenne (Belgium) and Federica Venturelli (Italy) won the TT. Karl Herzog (Germany) and Michiel Mouris (Netherlands) won the junior men’s road race and time-trial respectively and Paula Ostiz (Spain) doubled up in the junior women’s events. France’s elite sextet topped the standings in the mixed relay ahead of Italy while Norway took home the gold in the junior field.

UEC European Road Championships 2026 key information

  • Dates: Friday 2nd – Wednesday 7th October 2026
  • Location: Ljubljana, Slovenia
  • TV coverage: HBO Max, Eurosport, YouTube

UEC European Road Championships 2026 schedule

Day 1: Friday 2nd October

  • Women U23 Road Race
  • Men U23 Road Race

Day 2: Saturday 3rd October

  • Men Junior Road Race
  • Women Elite Road Race

Day 3: Sunday 4th October

  • Women Junior Road Race
  • Men Elite Road Race

Day 4: Tuesday 6th October

  • Junior TTT Mixed Relay
  • Elite TTT Mixed Relay

Day 5: Wednesday 7th October

  • Women Junior Time-Trial
  • Men Junior Time-Trial
  • Women U23 Time-Trial
  • Women Elite Time-Trial
  • Men Elite Time-Trial

UEC European Road Championships 2026 routes

U23 Women Road Race, 88.4km

All the road races take place on or finish on a 22.1km circuit around Šenčur, 14 miles north of Ljubljana. The circuit features 367m of elevation via the big climb to Možjanca, which comes after 5km and has a maximum gradient of 15.8%. The U23 women will cover four laps to total 88.4km and 1,616m of elevation.

U23 Men Road Race, 141.9km

The U23 men’s peloton will begin in the centre of Ljubljana and head northwest towards Škofja Loka over a flat parcours, crossing the Sava river south of Kranj to arrive at the Šenčur circuit. They will take on three laps for a total of 1,698m of elevation over 141.9km.

Junior Men Road Race, 110.5km

It’s five laps of the circuit with no dillydallying for the junior men, amassing 2,020m of elevation gain over 110.5km.

Elite Women Road Race, 130km

For the elite women, the race begins in Ljubljana for 85.8km of leg-softening prior to their arrival at the Šenčur circuit. They’ll complete just two laps over a short 130km, with 1,359m of elevation.

Junior Women Road Race, 66.3km

Three laps await the junior women, totalling 66.3km and 1,212m of elevation.

Elite Men Road Race, 196.3km

Just like the U23 men and elite women, the elite men will depart from Ljubljana and cover 85.8km before taking on five laps of the circuit. Over 196.3km the elevation gain totals 2,571m, so expect tired legs by the end.

Junior and Elite Mixed Relay, 44.3km

Back to the Šenčur circuit for the TTs. The men and women will complete one lap each in the mixed relay, totalling 44.3km.

All Individual Time-Trials, 22.1km

All the individual time-trials take place on the same day, with everyone completing one 22.1km lap of the same course as all the other events.

UEC European Road Championships 2026 elite favourites

With the European Championships providing a punchy route just after the World Championships, we can look at form from Canada to decipher who will be in the mix in Slovenia. In the men’s road race, look for Remco Evenepoel, who didn’t possess the legs expected of him in the road race after winning gold in the time-trial, plus (probably) Slovenia’s best hope of home glory Primož Roglič, Mads Pedersen, Giulio Ciccone and Juan Ayuso.

Demi Vollering couldn’t complete the solo breakaway she wanted in the fight for rainbows. Could that provide some extra motivation for the defending champion? Looking to dethrone her will be Elisa Longo Borghini and Marlen Reusser, who finished third and fourth in the World Championships. Keep an eye on Paula Blasi, Franzi Koch, Juliette Berthet and Cedrine Kerbaol too.

In the men’s TT, it’s expected that Jakob Söderqvist, Primož Roglič, Mathias Vacek, Bruno Armirail, Ethan Hayter and Callum Thornley should be eyeing the European jersey, with World Champ Evenepoel seemingly skipping this one. Maybe his name is just late to the start list. On the women’s side World Champion Marlen Reusser is the big favourite, with Elisa Longo Borghini and Cédrine Kerbaol likely to be her closest challengers.

How to watch the UEC European Road Championships 2026

The U23 and elite road races and elite individual time-trials will be broadcast on HBO Max in the UK and Eurosport across Europe. In Belgium, it’s VRT 1; in France it’s L’Equipe; in Italy it’s Rai; in Slovenia it’s TV Slovenija 2; in Switzerland it’s SSR (streaming) and RSI LA 2. The UEC will broadcast the junior events on their YouTube channel.

UK broadcast start times

Day 1: Friday 2nd October

  • Women U23 Road Race: 08:48 (HBO Max)
  • Men U23 Road Race: 14:37 (HBO Max)

Day 2: Saturday 3rd October

  • Men Junior Road Race: 09:50 (UEC YouTube)
  • Women Elite Road Race: 12:20 (HBO Max)

Day 3: Sunday 4th October

  • Women Junior Road Race: 08:50 (UEC YouTube)
  • Men Elite Road Race: 11:15 (HBO Max)

Day 4: Tuesday 6th October

  • Junior TTT Mixed Relay: 10:00 (UEC YouTube)
  • Elite TTT Mixed Relay: 14:15

Day 5: Wednesday 7th October

  • All individual time-trials: 08:15 (UEC YouTube)
  • Elite Women Individual Time-Trial: 13:00 (HBO Max)
  • Elite Men Individual Time-Trial: 14:30 (HBO Max)

UEC European Road Championships 2025 winners

  • Elite Men Road Race: Tadej Pogačar (Slovenia)
  • Elite Women Road Race: Demi Vollering (Netherlands)
  • Elite Men Time-Trial: Remco Evenepoel (Belgium)
  • Elite Women Time-Trial: Marlen Reusser (Switzerland)
  • U23 Men Road Race: Jarno Widar (Belgium)
  • U23 Women Road Race: Paula Blasi (Spain)
  • U23 Men Time-Trial: Jonathan Vervenne (Belgium)
  • U23 Women Time-Trial: Federica Venturelli (Italy)
  • Junior Men Road Race: Karl Herzog (Germany)
  • Junior Women Road Race: Paula Ostiz (Spain)
  • Junior Men Time-Trial: Michiel Mouris (Netherlands)
  • Junior Women Time-Trial: Paula Ostiz (Spain)
  • Elite Mixed Team Time-Trial: France
  • Junior Mixed Team Time-Trial: Norway

entry.title: Join the Gaza Sunbirds in October for The Great Ride of Return Series
entry.content:
The Gaza Sunbirds, Palestine’s para-cycling team of amputee athletes turned humanitarian aid organization, are working to support multiple rides this October in Wisconsin through local ride hosts, Great Ride MKE. Its goal is to bring people together through cycling and community and build solidarity. Find out how you can host one and where your local rides in the Wisconsin area will be happening…

The Great Ride of Return Series

The Great Ride of Return, a name and mission heavily inspired by the Great March of Return protests, uplifts the story of Sunbirds co-founder Alaa Al-Dali, an Olympic cycling hopeful who lost his leg after being shot by a sniper with an explosive round during the 2018 demonstrations.

The movement brings together thousands of participants across more than 95 cities and 35 countries who take to the streets in a showing of solidarity. Events aim to raise awareness for Palestinian mobility justice, demand an end to the occupation, and raise funds for essential aid distribution and disability rehabilitation in Gaza.

These rides are inspired by the courage and bravery of the Gaza Sunbirds. Participants of all ages gather to cycle peacefully, raise the Palestinian flag, and fund essential support for displaced families and disability rehabilitation. What began as solidarity rides has blossomed into an international campaign that merges the Sunbirds’ commitment to justice and inclusion with a collective call for freedom and peace.

Cycling stands at the heart of the Gaza Sunbirds story: wheels mean mobility, freedom, resilience, and non‑violent action. By cycling in solidarity, participants echo the Sunbirds—para‑athletes riding through adversity—and share that message of hope globally.

A Stayer Gaza Sunbirds prototype bike, which included a carbon fiber sleeve and metal armature, debuted at the 2025 Bespoked UK showcase 

While not all rides are fundraisers, many of these local rides also raise money. Hosts will link to the ongoing JustGiving fundraiser to collect donations. These contributions support humanitarian aid—food, hygiene kits, shelter—and para‑cycling gear in Gaza.

Funds help deliver essentials and empower amputee athletes striving to rebuild their lives.

October Rides in Milwaukee Hosted by Great Ride MKE

On October 11th, a slow-roll solidarity ride will meet at Urban Park Green Space (near Discovery World) at 1 PM.

On October 17th, there will be an advanced ride from Milwaukee to Madison, meeting at the Mitchell Park Domes at 10 AM

If your organization is hosting rides, please drop a link to them in the comments, and we’ll add them to this post. If you’re interested in hosting a ride in your city, you can apply to organize a Great Ride of Return event at the Gaza Sunbirds.

entry.title: Cyclist magazine issue 179: on sale now
entry.content:
Cyclist
Cyclist magazine issue 179: on sale now

Cyclist magazine Issue 179, October 2026, is on sale now. Subscribe to Cyclist or buy issue 179 here.

Over 179 issues now, the Big Ride has been the centrepiece of Cyclist magazine – a long-form, photo-rich deep dive into a particularly special bike ride in a particularly special part of the world. As is the nature of these things, we’re constantly on the lookout for new locations, new roads, new adventures around which we can weave a new story to bring to you, our loyal readers.

And sometimes that can lead to the temptation to try to redefine what a ‘special bike ride’ actually is – some new way of combining human, bike, road and terrain that’s an improvement on what we’ve done before. But as our latest Big Ride in the October 2026 issue of Cyclist (available now on newsstands or from the Cyclist Store) shows, there really is no need.

We’ve made our way to the Peloponnese peninsula of mainland Greece, which greeted us with a mix of beautifully quiet roads, punchy climbs and spectacular sea views in a part of the world that’s steeped in rich history, vibrant local culture and geological marvels, and yet is a world away from the over-subscribed tourist hotspots of the Greek islands. Sun, sea and volcanoes – what’s not to like?

On the subject of history, you’ll struggle to find a richer repository of cycling history than can be seen at the Ghisallo Museum on the shores of Lake Como in Italy’s Lombardia. Its location adjacent to the famed Madonna del Ghisallo climb of Il Lombardia fame makes for the perfect two-wheeled pilgrimage to earn your right to take in the museum’s many attractions, which range from a near-70-strong collection of Giro maglia rosas to a set of post-World War 2 winner’s sashes from the Tour of Flanders and Gino Bartali’s Tour de France-winning bike from 1938. We pay a visit in our October 2026 issue and tell the bigger story behind six of the museum’s many treasures.

One man who never actually rode Il Lombardia during his two-decade pro career is Welshman Geraint Thomas – Tour de France winner, Olympic gold medallist and a key component in the all-conquering Sky/Ineos machine of the 2010s. He may now have hung up his wheels, but he’s still at the sharp end of the peloton in his new role this year as Netcompany Ineos’s director of racing. We pay Thomas a visit to talk through the challenges of his new job, from the involvement of AI in pro cycling to dealing with human tragedy within the team.

Sticking with storied names within the world of cycling, the Prova Integrale is one of those bikes that’s an icon less in terms of its sales figures or pro pedigree, and more in a ‘if you know, you know’ kind of way. A classically aesthetic marriage of the best of carbon and titanium bike engineering, hand-crafted and custom-made in Australia using techniques that include everything from 3D printing to finishing parts in a ceramic rock tumbler, it’s a worthy focus of the latest instalment in our Dream Bikes series.

Then for a complete change of scenery it’s off to Norway, where we take on an epic three-day gravel ride across the country’s mountainous interior. It’s a real rite of passage – stone trolls, ferries, reindeer stew, all-day rain, singletrack, serene lakeside tarmac… it’s all on the menu in this rugged Scandinavian riding adventure.

Elsewhere in the October 2026 issue, we have an interview with the legendary Eddy Merckx, climb the Col d’Èze of Paris-Nice fame and the character-filled Dunkery Beacon in Somerset, shine a deserved spotlight on London’s XO Cycles, which is giving ex-offenders the chance to make a new start as bike mechanics, and test out new bikes from Merida, MMR and Specialized.

There’s plenty more besides in the latest issue of Cyclist, so make sure to pick up your copy on newsstands or at the Cyclist Store or get a Cyclist magazine subscription to have every issue delivered free, straight to your door.

There are three levels of Cyclist subscriptions available. For access to the Cyclist Rides online archive, prices start at £19.95 for six months. For the Cyclist digital package, which includes the digital version of Cyclist magazine plus Cyclist Rides, prices start at £21.95 for six months. For the full Cyclist membership, which includes Cyclist print magazine, the digital version of Cyclist, and Cyclist Rides, prices start at £37.95 for six months.

entry.title: WTB Goes Wider, Faster, and Deeper with All-New CGR i28 Wheelset
entry.content:
WTB’s new i28 gravel wheelset is designed to deliver speed, comfort, and durability in equal measure. Featuring deeper carbon rims with a generous internal width and WTB’s advanced Frequency 7X hubs, WTB CGR i28 wheels are engineered to maximize the performance of modern wide gravel tires while providing the confidence to ride fast across everything from smooth gravel roads to rough, technical terrain.

 

WTB CGR i28 Quick Hits

  • Price
    • USD:  Front $850 / Rear $950 / Wheelset $1,800
    • EUR:  Front €727.45 / Rear €822.45 / Wheelset €1,549.90
    • GBP:  Front £563 / Rear £636 / Wheelset £1,199
  • 700c only
  • Standard non boost axles 12 x 100/142
  • 28mm inner width
  • Freehub bodies: XD/R, HG, MS
  • Weight:
    • Front: 644 g
    • Rear: 729 g

World Cup-Proven Hubs with Bigger Balls (Bearings)

At the heart of CGR wheels are WTB’s new race-tested and World Cup-proven Frequency 7X hubs. These state-of-the-art hubs feature a patent-pending hub/ratchet interface that sets a new standard in performance and reliability.

All WTB ratchets use a DLC (Diamond-Like Carbon) coating to deliver greater hardness and significantly lower friction than traditional hard chrome-plated drive systems. To build on this durability, the inner (hub side) ratchet ring keys into place with splines rather than threads, allowing the hubs to withstand over twice the torque of traditional designs without requiring specialist tools for servicing.

Frequency 7X hubs use larger than industry-typical Enduro bearings throughout, including durable freehub bearings that increase the load rating by up to 38% compared with competing rear hubs. This creates a stiffer axle assembly, improving reliability and reducing maintenance intervals. The hubs are fully sealed and rigorously tested to keep dirt and moisture out, making the Frequency 7X hubs ready for long days and demanding conditions.

Rims That Deliver

WTB’s innovation doesn’t stop at the hubs. CGR carbon rims are purpose-built for modern gravel, combining a 40mm-deep profile with a strategically tuned 28mm internal width.

An internal rim width of 28mm provides the ideal platform for 45-54mm gravel tires, balancing tire stability with the desired profile for traction, suppleness, and rolling efficiency. Wider rims can square off the tire, compromising its ability to perform as intended.

CGR i28 carbon rims also feature an asymmetric profile that helps balance spoke tension, while 4D spoke drillings and internally reinforced spoke beds optimize load distribution and overall wheel strength. Patented TCS technology completes the package, providing exceptional air retention for reliable tubeless performance.

Better Together

WTB’s CGR i28 is a gravel wheelset designed to complement the growing trend toward wider tires and rims, giving riders a stable and durable foundation for everything from fast gravel racing to long-distance adventures. Pair CGR i28 with WTB’s new aerodynamically optimized Byway RS 50, Course 52, Macro 54, or slightly narrower 45mm tires to unlock a new level of gravel performance.

Ride With Confidence

From burly enduro to lightweight gravel, WTB backs its carbon rims with our Ride With Confidence Guarantee. If you break a WTB carbon rim while riding, as long as you’re the original owner, we’ll send you a replacement for free. No exceptions.

Find out more at WTB

The post WTB Goes Wider, Faster, and Deeper with All-New CGR i28 Wheelset appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Brotherhood and Heartbreak on the Utah Backcountry Discovery Route – Karter Machen, Chris Burkard, Lachlan Morton, Mateo Paez, & Nate Sorenson
entry.content:
Lachlan Morton, Chris Burkard, Mateo Páez, Karter Machen, and Nate Sorenson experience the BDR together and recount the story from their own angle, from hard desert logistics to a first-time bikepacker’s shift from feeling out of his depth to pure joy. Pedaling nearly 800 miles from Evanston, Wyoming, to Monument Valley over ten days, each rider shares in the lesson that the people you travel with matter more than the place, and life can bring joy and sorrow in equal measure. Join the trip…

Lachlan

When the 6-minute voice message from Nate came through on WhatsApp, I knew he wasn’t interested in abandoning his north-south Utah route to join me on the Sierra Foothills route I’d put together. Upon listening to his explanation, I knew my route would have to wait. There was no question I’d be joining him on his mission.

Nate is one of my best mates. We met in Albania when he was capturing the action behind the camera, documenting the journey. In the years since, he has captured a lot of my longer rides. He has witnessed the raw reality of these efforts, the ugly parts, the parts that won’t make the cut when you’re in the business of romanticizing. But for whatever reason, this only fueled a fire within him to experience that for himself. He picked up his bike, built his fitness, and gained experience slowly. We’d done a couple of trips together in the saddle and even when we were having the greatest time, he was also taking notes, honing his experience in on something that was coming. I now knew this was it; this is what he was building toward. There was no way I could miss this. This was a celebration of the beautiful place he came from and the life he wants to lead, with no meat left on the bone.

The route itself intrigued me. Essentially, we’d be hopping between mountain ranges as we made our way south. These ‘small’ ranges would all be mountains of note where I grew up, but in the States they are shadowed by the grander peaks and divides that neighbor them. The mountains wouldn’t pose the biggest challenge – at higher elevations the temperature would be pleasant and the streams flowing. It was the dry, hot expanses that linked them that would provide the biggest obstacle.

The crew assembled was a list of guys I feel lucky to have as mates. Friendships this tight are easily bonded in childhood, when we’re more open, curious, and accepting. These friendships I have made as an adult, and as I get older, I’ve realized that is something special. With this group I could feel not only myself, but an open, capable, and free version that is only available to me when I feel completely comfortable. Both Chris and Karter I’d shared many miles with. Friends through chance, but forged in situations where true character is exposed and therefore, in this case, ensuring a lifelong bond. Mateo was new to me, but only in the sense that we hadn’t met. Of the same age, with wildly different paths in cycling, we shared an instant and deep connection on this route. As a child and adolescent, I took myself quite seriously, and due to that, I feel I missed my true band of brothers. The kind of friends that get into trouble, laugh, and hold each other accountable. With this group I found that, and there was no one else I’d rather be on the journey with.

Whilst we made good pace, calculated water carries and had our resupplies locked in, there was never any hesitation to stop and jump in a river, make some peanut butter tortillas, or fire up the burner for a coffee. We travelled over a vast distance, but none of it was lost on us; we took it all in. There was an unspoken knowing that for us, this is what life is truly about, and we soaked in every moment.

Deep into the trip, I noticed a look in Nate’s eyes that was familiar to me. A man on the edge of his physical capability, wringing the towel dry. The only difference between what I have experienced in this moment and the way he was experiencing it was that he never for a second let it diminish what he was experiencing. He had a presence of mind that ensured he knew that’s what he was there for, and having reached it, he wasn’t going to shy away from that experience for a second.

My takeaway from this trip was simply to make time to go sleep in the dirt with your mates. Our modern lives make it all too easy to be too busy. But for me now it feels a lot clearer. These experiences take commitment; you have to make the time, cut some ambition, and allow yourself to be that kid who just wants to go ride bikes with his friends. I came away from this trip with not only a cup full of renewed motivation and ideas but a greater appreciation for the experience we can have just viewing the world that exists around us and how much better that is when you share it with mates.

Mateo

We met up with the boys at mile 102 in Evanston, Wyoming. It was the second Friday in June. If you follow bikepacking or ultra racing in general, you know this date is an important one. I was more than glad to be out on the road again, loaded bike, not racing, and staring down the vast expanse of the Great Basin on this particular day.

Joining an 800-mile, statewide crossing of a bikepacking trip with strangers is a questionable decision. I have ridden with Chris enough to trust him. We have grown to become close friends through bikepacking. Meeting in Iceland, riding the Monumental Loop, packrafting in Utah, and always scheming something 12 months out of the year. I think I can trust Lachlan’s ability to handle himself in the backcountry. Karter, well, he’s been vouched for by the rest of them. Nate is a total gem of a rad dad and a historian of his home state of Utah. I just met him too. Simple as that, Nate wanted to ride across Utah, and I was lucky enough to be invited as a pre-approved stranger.

I never doubted our ability as a group but quickly learned that this is a huge deal for two of the 5 guys. For Karter, this is his first off-road bikepacking trip. First time riding a mountain bike, and on a borrowed one at that. For Nate, this might be his fifth bikepacking trip? I sure couldn’t tell without them telling me. Their setups are dialed, confidence is oozing, and we have a lot of rugged country to get through. I just assumed that if these guys can hang with Lach then we were good to go. As the days went on, I was thrilled to share anything that I know to help our fellow road dogs get to the end of this route.

We had daily goals; those turned into which petroglyphs to stop and see. This wasn’t all easy miles and casual resupplies, though. It took some calculated planning to make sure we could make it through some long desert stretches. Those stretches meant leaving at 4:00 am and taking long midday swim sessions in the Green and Colorado Rivers. A few big passes were joyous at elevation, but once we were in canyon country, I felt locked into a maze of sand, impassable cliffs, and heat.

A common thread among all of us: this appetite for slowing down. Bikepacking, my way of slowing down while constantly trying to speed up. Exploring new and familiar places, tying together once-traveled regions by bike with a new perspective. It gives me time and space to feel the landscape. It takes exposure to the elements for a couple of days, sleeping on the ground and waking up excited to eat at the gas station. Bikepacking is always hard at some point; it doesn’t matter where or how fast you ride, the challenge is part of it and the experience is always worth it.

I made it to day 7 of the 10. Then I had to get back to work in Oregon and catch a flight.

I left the boys at 4:00 am somewhere in the La Sal Range. I rode myself to Moab that morning, descending by the Fisher Towers at sunrise. It was bittersweet leaving them, knowing the hardest days were ahead and I wouldn’t be able to see my trusted road dogs make it to Monument Valley, the end of the line. As the days wore us down physically, our guards were stripped away. We strangers became bonded through overland travel, slowly but surely. Throughout this journey, I lost a friend to a drunk driver. She was hit while cycling home from dinner. I received the news midway through our ride. I didn’t talk about it much other than to Chris because it’s horribly sad and, to be honest, it hurt too much. Someone so bright, taken so swiftly doing something so simple, just riding home. On day four, Chris received a call that one of his close friends passed away in an accident doing something they love, someone we were with a month prior. This sparked quite a somber moment amongst all five of us in a shitty motel room in the middle of nowhere.

The harshest of reminders that these things we love – cycling, traveling, experiencing hardships and tailwinds – are better together with trusted friends who motivate you to be more than just a reliable travel partner on the bike. We inspire each other to be good humans.

Karter

When Nate, the man behind the route, first told me about the idea months before we left, I couldn’t quite wrap my head around it. Crossing Utah from north to south by mountain bike sounded equal parts ridiculous and intriguing. I agreed almost immediately.
At first it was just the two of us. Over the following months Lachlan, Chris, and Mateo joined the plan, and before long I found myself riding alongside people I’d admired for years. I was, without question, the least experienced of the group, and I felt completely out of my depth.

Then the first day arrived.

As soon as we started pedaling, most of that fear disappeared. I had some idea of what lay ahead – the terrain, the heat, the long days – but I had no idea the trip would become one of the most joyful and impactful experiences of my life.

Over the following days, each of the guys generously shared years of hard-earned knowledge, advice, and wisdom, always with a willingness to lend a hand when it was needed. I’d spent plenty of time riding with Lachlan and Nate over the years, and they’ve become two of my closest friends through our travels, but this was my first time getting to know Mateo and Chris. It didn’t take long to understand how I was in good company.

I thought I knew Utah, but man, was I wrong.

Moving through the state at the pace of a bicycle revealed an intimate version I’d never experienced before. The iconic red desert, alpine meadows, and high mountain passes before dropping us back into a heat so relentless and unforgiving that it’s almost impossible to describe. It’s something you simply have to experience.

There was something deeply satisfying about living by the rhythm of the sun, sleeping on the ground, cooling off in rivers whenever we found them, and watching the Milky Way stretch across the night sky. Those moments were unforgettable.

But when I look back now, it’s not the landscapes or the effort; it’s the time spent and connections made with such a good group of guys.

Life doesn’t stop simply because you’re on an adventure. During those ten days, some of us received heartbreaking news from home. Others, myself included, were quietly working through difficult seasons of life. We all carried something.

I’m grateful for the hours we spent together, for the climbs that turned into conversations, the swims that washed away the day’s heat, swollen eyes over morning coffees in dry washes, and the peanut butter and honey tortillas Lach graciously had prepared up the climbs. Those simple moments gave us the space to show up for one another.

More than an expedition across Utah, it became a reminder that the places we travel are often only half the story. It’s the people you experience them with.

The post Brotherhood and Heartbreak on the Utah Backcountry Discovery Route appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Ride Concepts Livewire Shoe Review – Sam Hodges
entry.content:
After blowing through pairs of MTB flat shoes every six months, Sam Hodges decided to give the Ride Concepts Livewire a try. Do the Livewire shoes hold up to daily thrashing on Moab’s techie trails? Read Sam’s review below…

Ride Concepts Livewire Quick Hits

  • $122
  • Colors: Charcoal (reviewed), Black, Olive
  • Sizes:
    • Men’s: 7-15
    • Women’s: 5-10
  • High Grip rubber outsole
  • Cup outsole is glued and stitched for durability and delivers ultimate pedal feel
  • Dual-density EVA insole provides additional support and cushioning
  • Traditional lace closure
  • Anti-bacterial mesh lining controls odor
  • TPU toe and heel protection with reinforced anti-abrasion film
  • Fully gusseted tongue
  • Outsole medial arch provides additional support for impact damping and power transfer
  • 400g per shoe (size M9)

About ten years ago, I started transitioning from climbing as my main form of recreation to biking; five years before that, I had transitioned from skateboarding to climbing. Backpacking has been a consistent form of getting outside between all of these activities. I still dabble in skating, climbing, and now backpack for a living. I’ve also added several new forms of recreation: packrafting, trail running, canyoneering, search and rescue, along with road biking, gravel biking, mountain biking, and bikepacking. It’s sick that for each of these activities, there is a specific shoe you need (or want) to do each of them comfortably or more efficiently. The downside is that shoes are expensive and don’t seem to be getting cheaper any time soon.

Like most people, after getting over the initial hurdle of buying a bike and all the other gear to start riding, I thought, “Surely one of the pairs of shoes I already own MUST be able to do double duty biking.” I shredded multiple pairs of skate and running shoes before moving on to approach shoes, which lasted a little longer (but not by much). A couple years into riding as my primary activity, I finally gave in and purchased some mountain bike-specific shoes, adding yet another pair of shoes to the ever-growing arsenal. Since then I’ve largely stuck with 5.10 Freerider Pros, after being disappointed by the longevity and grip I found with other options on the market in my earlier days of riding. The aggressive and technical style in Moab and my preference for flats means that I’m going through about two pairs a year. After about a decade of riding almost daily, I figured it might be time to branch out. In the last five years, the market for shoes has expanded with a wider range of rubber compounds and more intentional styles being developed. After hearing good things from friends and being drawn in by the slimmed-down and low-profile aesthetics, I decided to test out the Ride Concepts Livewire flat pedal shoes.

The Livewire is a slim skate-style shoe (which isn’t easy to accomplish with molded heel and toe protection) and doesn’t fall into either the heavily padded downhill or more athletic hiker style categories. The soles feature a Ride Concepts High Grip rubber compound, which I found to be slightly stiffer and more durable than other options I’ve ridden. The sole of the Livewire has a slightly raised honeycomb pattern, which allows for pedal pins to grip easily and the shoes to find their place without feeling forced or needing to constantly readjust for better grip. That said, they also don’t feel so locked in that readjustments are difficult. While I enjoyed the feel on the bike, hiking in them is a different experience. I found myself slipping around and unable to get good footing when hiking on packed trails or on sandstone slick rock. The fully gusseted tongue prevents rocks and dirt from getting into the shoe when hiking or biking, which is a huge plus. It’s pretty annoying having to stop to empty out your shoes when biking. Due to the gusseted tongue, they can feel a little warm and constricting. This wasn’t a dealbreaker for me, since I like my shoes to feel tight around my feet, but that might not be everyone’s preference.

I’ve put these shoes through their paces over the last 7 months and have been pleased overall. Riding in Moab, I spend the majority of my time on singletrack out of the saddle, climbing or descending technical rocky trails. Between the terrain, distance, and riding style, the sole of these shoes lasted longer than expected. The RC Livewire has blown past my typical 6-month timeline and still has a good amount of life in them. The price point of the RC Livewire is another huge benefit, as I’m used to spending $40.00 more per pair. One of the best things you can say about a shoe is that I never found myself thinking about them. They fit true to size, feel secure around my feet and on the pedals, and I haven’t felt my feet fatiguing during longer, more demanding rides. The grip and stiffness of the sole exceeded what I have come to expect from a modern MTB-specific shoe. Overall, I am impressed with the durability and price point. If you find yourself needing to add yet another pair of shoes to your collection that won’t break the bank, these will look good, and you might be pleasantly surprised by how long they last.

Pros

  • Cheaper than most flat pedal shoes at $122.00
  • Durable soles that provide exceptional grip
  • Low-profile design and neutral colorways that look good on the trail.
  • True to size, with sizes ranging from 7-15, including half sizes.

Cons

  • Not the best in grip for longer hike-a-bike adventures.
  • Can feel a little warm because of the fully gusseted tongue.
  • Narrow fit.

The post Ride Concepts Livewire Shoe Review appeared first on The Radavist.
