entry.title: 10 Years of Starling Cycles
entry.content:
Making it for 10 years as a steel mountain bike company ain’t easy, especially when all the marketing in the bike industry is seemingly pushing you down. What the lads at Starling Cycles have created is the very definition of legacy. They’ve innovated through simplicity, leading a paradigm shift in metal full suspension bikes and helping usher in a worldwide movement of workshed-built shred sleds. This year, Starling Cycles celebrates a decade of counter culture. Read on for a note from its founder Joe McEwan below along with some photos John shot in 2025 while visiting the shop in Bristol…

Joe, founder of Starling Cycles here,

This year marks a full decade of Starling Cycles. Ten years since I quit my job in aerospace and started building mountain bike frames full time in my shed at the bottom of my garden.

It started a bit before the ten year mark, somewhere around 2013. I had a busy aerospace job and two young kids, and I loved escaping to my garden shed in the evenings to unwind. I went on a frame building course, I began hoovering up all the equipment I could find, kitting out the shed and making frames for my kids. Pretty soon I was creating proper full suspension frames that I could ride, and then the same for my friends. I learned loads and was getting pretty comfortable making tough, reliable and simple bike frames.

Then one day, around 2016, my project working on A380s, came to an end. My boss sat me down and said “Joe, I reckon you’d much rather be building bike frames” and I knew straight away he was right. Goodbye cushy corporate job and stable salary, hello Starling Cycles. I set up the company and dived in headfirst.

Pretty quickly, the mountain bike media got wind of it and were really supportive. Steve Jones of Dirt Mag rode my Murmur prototype and said it was the fastest thing he’d ridden all year. It just grew and grew from there. In 2018, I moved out of the shed into a bigger workshop, hired staff, moved again, evolved the design of the frame, and then moved again and here we are.

“Here” looks like 1500+ frames in the wild, all over the world. We have new customers finding us every day and joining the family. We have heaps of gen 1 and 2 frames out there, still going strong. We have a small network of dealers, we’re growing in Germany, loads of Americans love our bikes. We have two amazing partners helping us to manufacture our frames, in Taiwan and Czechia. All whilst still managing to build frames at home in Bristol, despite the odds.

I’m not going to pretend it’s been, or is, easy. Building niche bikes out of niche materials in a niche way is bloody hard work. We’ve had Covid, we’ve seen the rise of the eBikes, we’ve seen endless cheap bikes flood the market and heaps of amazing businesses with beautiful bikes fail. All that with the usual day to day ups and downs of running a business. The pool of people enjoying the hard graft of a human-powered pedal bike seems to be getting smaller and smaller, let alone a simple, sustainable, long-lasting and slightly weird one!

But we’re here and doing it our way. We’re making simple, beautiful bikes that last for years and can be repaired, refurbished and repainted. I hope that’s played a part in why we’re still here and (hopefully) will be here for plenty more.

What does the future look like for Starling? I hope it holds plenty more simple, beautiful bikes. No motors, no fragile materials, no marketing bullshit. An alternative to over-complicated, throw away products. Plenty of fun and not taking ourselves too seriously. It’d be nice to grow a little, but not at the expense of doing things our way or getting up to our eyeballs in debt. Beyond that, you’ll have to watch this space. When I know, I’ll let you know.

All ideas welcome!

Thanks to everyone that’s made Starling possible for a decade. Our customers, our staff past and present, our suppliers, dealers and partners. And to everyone that’s ever left a comment saying our swingarms look too skinny and our bikes are crap.

We love you lot!

See more at Starling Cycles.

The post 10 Years of Starling Cycles appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Sophie Allen’s Field Notes
entry.content:
Kona / WTB rider Sophie Allen is hard to put in a box. She races, dirt jumps, explores, gets competitive, gets easily distracted by wildlife and generally seems pretty happy as long as she’s outside.

Hailing from California, Sophie has built a reputation as a seriously versatile rider, but racing is only part of the picture. She’s also a biologist, climber, hiker and all-round outdoor lover, with a genuine curiosity for the places she rides through and the things that live there. That connection to the outdoors is also a big part of why Sophie has recently joined Protect Our Winters as a POW Athlete Ambassador, using her platform as a rider to help advocate for the places and seasons she loves.

We teamed up with acclaimed filmmaker and fellow Californian Brian Vernor to get an insight into what makes Sophie tick, and to spend some time with her away from the start line. The film lands alongside POW’s Stoke the Vote campaign, which is encouraging the outdoor community to get involved and use its collective voice to help protect the places we love to ride, ski, climb and explore.

entry.title: Wolf Tooth Alt Performance Pedals
entry.content:
The Wolf Tooth family of pedals continues to expand. The Minnesota-based manufacturer’s new Taiwan-made ALT Performance XC Pedals are at a lower price point than its ALT US-made pedals…

The ALT Performance pedals bring the same carefully designed shoe-to-pedal contact, low stack, and light weight to a lower price point for the first time. ALT is the brand’s first pedal model available in all three product tiers: the original Premium, US-made series ALT, the ultralight race-focused ALT MKØ, and now a Taiwan-made ALT Performance.

Alt Performance Quick Hits

  • $159.95 USD
  • Made in Taiwan
  • 326g / pair
  • 534 mm² contact area
  • 15mm pedal thickness
  • Fixed 55mm q-factor
  • Forged and post-machined pedal bodies
  • Satin chrome-plated chromoly steel axles and hardware
  • Available in five Color Shop finishes: Black, Raw Silver, Orange, Gold, and Red

Performance Series components were first rolled out in 2020, when we introduced Premium and Performance Series Headsets. These were followed up earlier this year with the launch of its CTRL Performance clipless and Waveform Performance flat pedals.

ALT Performance XC Pedals are designed for trail MTB riding, gravel, and ‘cross racing. These pedals are light and thin with a low stack height, and feature more platform area than the competition for better control and maximum power transfer. The open center between the cages gives these pedals increased mud-shedding capabilities when the weather isn’t on your side; they feature durable hard chrome-plated chromoly axles, fully SPD-compatible bindings, and a non-adjustable 55mm Q factor.

ALT Performance XC Pedals are designed in Minnesota, USA, made in Taiwan, and available in six Color Shop anodized finishes: Black, Red, Orange, Gold, and Raw Silver. Retail pricing is $159.95 USD / pair. Available now on wolftoothcomponents.com and via its network of dealers and distributors worldwide.

The post Wolf Tooth Alt Performance Pedals appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Cinelli Tutto Mini Mike Giant Edition
entry.content:
Cinelli‘s Tutto Mini is the Italian brand’s mini velo and it just rolled out a Mike Giant collaboration edition (€3.500) that caught our eye with its MUSA parts build kit…

Mike Giant and Cinelli’s collaborative relationship goes back to the early aughts when the artist was living in San Francisco. Throwing it back to that original collab, the artist designed the Cinelli Icons artwork. The Icons artwork features drawings and text laid out like a tattoo flash sheet around his coiled snake and the winged C. He originated the “drawn on” frame aesthetic that’s been popularized today.

The Tutto Mini is made from Columbus Cromor steel and comes rolling on 20″ wheels with a shorter wheelbase and a vintage Fat Chance-inspired segmented fork crown. There are adjustable disc brake slider dropouts for fixed, singlespeed or geared setups, and belt-drive compatible with 19 eyelets for racks, bags and cargo.

Cinelli and Mike worked to spec a largely MUSA build kit for this premium spec including Paul Components Klampers, Love Levers and Boxcar stem, with White Industries square taper cranks (170 mm) with 48T ENO chainring, bottom bracket, plus EC34 headset and seat collar in red. For rubber, its rolling on Maxxis Holy Roller 20 x 2.2″ tires, brings the bar height up with Stay Strong cruiser bars, a the cherry on top is the classic Cinelli Volare saddle.

Frames are available in size Small or Large.

See more of the Mike Giant complete at Cinelli, which is also available as a frameset for €1.500. There’s also a full capsule collection you can browse at Cinelli.

The post Cinelli Tutto Mini Mike Giant Edition appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Adidas Freerider MTB Shoes Get Stripes
entry.content:
Today, Adidas unveils the next generation of its Freerider mountain bike shoes, featuring Pro Boa Flat and Pro Boa Clipless models. And with new stripes, the iconic brand is known for…

The Freerider debuted in 2009 with its Stealth rubber construction being lauded by professional racers and novices alike. The arrival of the Five Ten Hellcat clipless model soon followed, and by 2010 the shoe had already been fully welcomed by the cultural zeitgeist. Then, in 2011, Five Ten and adidas joined forces.

Now, the next wave of Adidas mountain bike shoes brings together these defining franchises, uniting Five Ten’s shoe designs’ grip, fit, and off-the-bike style with the Hellcat clip-in performance. The Freerider will be available as a laced flat pedal version, Pro Boa flat pedal, and Pro Boa Clipless.

The new Freerider range starts at €120 / $120, with the Freerider Pro Boa and the Freerider Pro Boa Clipless priced at €180/$180 and €250/$250 respectively. Available to buy at adidas.com and via the adidas app from March 2027.

See more at Adidas.

entry.title: COGTINUUM: 2500 KM Through the Desert on All Gravel Fixed Gears – Donnet Dumas & Stan Engelbrecht
entry.content:
Stan Engelbrecht and three friends are about to take four custom-built steel fixed-gear bicycles along an all-gravel backroads route from the center of Namibia to Cape Town. They’re calling the adventure COGTINUUM. Read on for Stan’s description of the project below accompanied by beautiful 35 mm film photos from Stan Engelbrecht and Donnet Dumas. Hop on, it’s gonna be a wild ride…

It started with a dream in July 2024. An actual dream, dreamt while sleeping in a tent, under a huge tree whose branches dripped with scorpions, in a dried-up riverbed in Namibia.

A few days later, as we drove over the crest of the Fish River Canyon and dipped onto the flat, moonscape heading back home, I finally spoke the dream aloud …

Eventually, that weird dream, with me stuck in a support car feverishly trying to get out to join my friend Nkosi as he flew through the desert, mashed together with a few other ideas that had been grinding around in my head for a while. And on 8 October 2024, a late-night text to my friend and fellow fixed gear rider Nick McIntyre laid out the bare bones:

Four riders.

Fixed gears.

Steel frames.

No brakes.

Iron ore train.

Namibia to Cape Town.

Who could pass on that? Now we just needed some more riders. And the bikes. And some money. (And a whole lot of other shit, it would turn out).

For over a year I emailed out the proposal document to many, many, many companies, collaborators, photographers, filmmakers… pretty much anyone, to see if someone would get on board with us:

“I’m writing to you about a bit of a crazy project … myself and a handful of experienced and dedicated fixed gear riders are undertaking a month-long 2500km ride from the little town of Omaruru in the centre of Namibia all the way to Cape Town, South Africa. We’ll be crossing the red dunes of Sossusvlei, past the Fish River Canyon, Aussenkehr, the Orange River, the Richtersveld mountains, and the desolate South African West Coast on custom-built fixed gear gravel bicycles. It will be an awesome adventure”

Sossusvlei Dunes

It took many conversations to help explain the ‘why’ behind this. Because ‘I had a dream’ doesn’t really cut it in the real world. And eventually I was able to put it into words:

“I’m a long-time steel frame and fixed gear rider, and on a recent touring trip along the remote South African West Coast I encountered the legendary 4-kilometer-long Sishen-Saldanha cargo train that takes iron ore from the interior to the coast for export. This surreal sight led me to make a conceptual link between the physical iron ore and the steel bicycle I was riding, and  the fascinating process that connects these two states of steel …”

 Fish River Canyon

“The overarching theme of the project is the recyclable resource that is steel, and particularly bicycle frame builders that use steel. We will be telling the story of the iron ore that is extracted from the African landscape we’ll traverse, its journey to foundries around the world where it becomes bicycle frame tubing, and how that tubing, in this case, is returned to become bicycle frames, built specifically by Southern African frame builders. These steel frames will become the bicycles we ride from Omaruru to Cape Town. In part, the project aims to highlight the benefits of choosing a steel frame over a carbon frame, while at the same time highlighting the skills of some Southern-African frame builders.”

And the builders are who this is really all about. Ex-Saffron builder Matthew Sowter, a South African based in London, was the first to get on board. He and I worked together on the first frame, getting all the quirky measurements and clearances out of the way for the rest.

David Mercer of Mercer in Cape Town, South Africa, was an obvious choice; I own two of his bikes already. And David always knows I am up to something.

David and Kai

With a bit more digging, I was able to find Zimbabwean Carlos Santa Clara of Santa Clara Bikes (recent recipient of the SRAM Bespoked Inclusivity Sponsorship), based in Lisbon, Portugal. He was in.

And finally, a late entry of new builder Kai Pringle of The Bellum Project, also based in Cape Town, rounded up the builders group nicely. Kai is also going to ride his frame on the trip.

Each of these builders committed to building a steel gravel fixed gear frame with a steel fork.

Which is where Reynolds came in. They generously sponsored the tubing and paved the way to get the project up and running. From the beginning, I had a clear idea of what these bikes should look like.

Sowter details

Conceptually, I foresaw the bikes paying somewhat of a homage to the early track bikes that made it out of the velodromes and onto the city streets around the world in the 1980’s. Paired with components with a classic nod, it would complement the project perfectly. I was seeing these parts with a polished finish, reflecting the arid desert and blue skies of the Namib spectacularly. As for the paintwork, we settled on the idea of leaving them completely unpainted, raw. Letting them rust and patina all the way down to Cape Town. A way to track the passage of time on the raw material. Steel being the star of the show, after all.

Richterveldt Road

Now the hunt was on to spec the frames with nowadays really rare matching all-silver components. Rim manufacturer Astral was the first to see the potential of how beautiful a fully polished rim could look out in the desert. Loren from Astral really got it, and through a massive effort was able to get the rim sets hand-polished for all our bikes. To assist with our tyre clearance issues was Paul Components and their super niche, super beautiful, super polished wider spaced fixed gear hub sets. Ritchey, Alter, Miche, and White Industries were the next obvious choices as manufacturers that still offered anything other than all-black.

Ultradynamico, Fizik, Tailfin and Izumi took our desert rig builds to the next level.

Map Planning

We spent months waiting for all the frames to be completed. And weeks were spent agonizing over the route, planning the most spectacular way down with deconstructed atlases stuck up on a wall. We got together to build wheels, fit tyres, and try out components.

David brazing and wheel building

An all-gravel fixed gear is totally new territory. And we had no idea how these frames would ride. For all we knew, they could be complete dogs. But we had flights and accommodation booked. So… Ha ha! Thank fuck they ride like absolute WHIPS!

Small human in landscape

The project is called COGTINUUM. We’ll be crossing the desert along an all-gravel 2,500 km route on these things. We start on 1 October 2026. This is just the beginning. Follow the adventure over on Instagram.

The post COGTINUUM: 2500 KM Through the Desert on All Gravel Fixed Gears appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Gravel Racing: Family Events – Two Kids, a Wife, and a Bike in a Van – Miguel Ovalles
entry.content:
Miguel from The Radavist’s Race Metal series has been racing gravel for the last two years. This time, he’s trying to figure out if he can bring his whole family along for race weekends without breaking the bank. For Gravel Worlds 300, Miguel, his wife Susan, and their two kids travel to Nebraska in a Wayfarer van and camp right at the venue.

But bringing the family comes with a question: can he still properly prepare, get enough rest, and race 300 miles when being a dad doesn’t exactly come with a guaranteed good night’s sleep?

At the same time, having his family there gives Miguel something he doesn’t get when racing alone. Knowing they’re waiting for him at the finish line might be the extra motivation he needs to keep pushing and get back to them faster. So, can he race 300 miles and still be a present dad and husband in between? Follow along as Miguel balances family life, race preparation, and 300 miles of Nebraska gravel at Gravel Worlds.

Thanks to Wayfarer for setting Miguel up with a van for the 2026 Gravel Worlds! Check out the Wayfarer van conversion they used here.

entry.title: Rockgeist Silver Spacelink
entry.content:
The Spacelink by North Carolina-based Rockgeist allows you to easily attach both top tube and feed/stem bags to your bike by replacing a stem spacer on 1 1/8″ steerer bicycle forks. This comes in handy for feed bags, particularly on hardtail or mountain bike frames where a short, 35 mm stem doesn’t have enough purchase to have a velcro strap wrapped around it. After years of requests, the team at Rockgeist has finally made a silver Spacelink ($38), and they’re in stock for now at Rockgeist.

entry.content:
Introducing PNW Components‘ minimalist grip: the new Range grips. They feature micro-fins on top, waffling underneath, and a soft-but-structured compound for 100% cushy vibes when the trail turns to chonk…

Range Grips Quick Hits

  • Sizes: Regular, XL
  • Diameter: Regular 30mm, XL 35mm
  • MSRP: $29 USD
  • Colors: Blackout Black, Peanut Butter, Hyper Lichen, Safety Orange, Fruit Snacks, Cement Grey
  • Compound: Proprietary Thermoplastic Rubber, 25A Durometer
  • Weight: 90g Regular / 134g XL Clamp: Closed-end, single-clamp

Features

Micro Fins: The Range Grip features a micro-fin pattern that supports your hand by allowing it to sink into the upper section of the grip; this provides an ultra-supple hand feel on spicy terrain.

Waffle House: On the underside of this grip, we designed a grid pattern that your fingertips can really dig into, with a raised waffle section for that extra bite.

Durometer: The Range’s proprietary thermoplastic rubber comes in a 25A durometer. We’ve tested four or five compounds over the years and keep coming back to this one for its blend of cushiness and durability.

A Recycled Core: The plastic core on the Range Grip is constructed from 80% recycled fishing nets and other reclaimed maritime plastic.

Small Fry, Big Fry: The Range comes in two sizes. The Regular (30mm) runs thin for a supple feel that stays plugged into the trail, while the XL (35mm), favored by riders with larger hands, adds extra cushion on top of the already supple patterning.

See more at PNW Components.

entry.title: Garmin Acquires Moxy, and Garmin Gets Sued
entry.content:
Today I’ve got two tidbits in the sports tech world on the Garmin front that I thought were notable. Both happened over the last few days. So, let’s dive right into it.

Garmin’s Moxy Acquisition:


(Above, an older Moxy sensor next to a Garmin chest strap pod for size scale)

Garmin has acquired Moxy, the muscle oxygen sensor company. But I’d argue the acquisition has some notable backstory to it, with the two companies seemingly in a friends-with-benefits relationship for more than a decade.

First though, Garmin has indeed confirmed the acquisition, stating simply:

“Garmin can confirm its acquisition of Moxy Monitor, but we have no further comment at this time.”

That short of a statement is actually quite unusual for Garmin, which makes numerous acquisitions each year. Most of the time, they issue a press release with a bit of hype for the acquired company, some executive statements, and then some wording that states everyone at the acquired company has places within Garmin. Concurrently, the acquired company then issues their own e-mails to existing customers, stating some variant of “all is good for now, stay the course”. This pattern is tried and true for Garmin, such as recently with the Garmin acquisition of TrainingPeaks.

But this time…oddly nothing.

I’m not yet sure what to make of that shortness, but in the meantime, a few historical notables. Though less historical, here’s what a Moxy sensor looks like these days, taken last summer at Eurobike:

Moxy has been around quite some time, and actually has quite a close relationship with Garmin and historically with ANT+ (which Garmin owns/owned). Moxy first announced with early ANT+ support back in January 2014, and then was featured at the ANT+ Symposium in September 2014 when Garmin announced the existence of Connect IQ. Then just months later Moxy was featured as the first Connect IQ app on Garmin watches. Followed by a year later when Moxy actually got their Muscle Oxygen profile through ANT+ certification, and directly onto Garmin watches (no Connect IQ app required). That was a big deal at the time, when new profiles onto new devices was basically unheard of. All the while Moxy was battling it out with BSX for the muscle oxygen realm, albeit that didn’t last long as BSX folded (and Moxy stepped-in to offer deals for BSX users).

From that point forward, Moxy slowly shifted more towards coaches and academic usage, rather than focusing on consumers directly. Certainly, consumers could purchase their devices, but that wasn’t really the focus area. For the most part, Moxy just continued to build a stable business without crazy amounts of flair.

And for those who know Roger Schmitz (seen below), the CEO and founder behind Moxy – that’s always been the case. He’s an easygoing guy focused on science and fitness, and less on frills and marketing. Probably one of the nicest guys in sports tech. The sensor package costs exactly the same as it did back in 2018 (for real, I just looked up the prices in my old pieces), though the device has improved a bit here and there every few years with slightly updated versions. All of this is, of course, at relatively small production levels. They certainly aren’t making 50,000 devices per year.

(The above is Roger and I in 2014 at the ANT+ Symposium, where he had convinced me to suffer during a test. Also, I’m apparently 12 years old. And while I could have found a nicer/better/newer photo, I feel like this nostalgic photo is a bit of a fun test of your sports tech founder knowledge. Points awarded if you can name them all. The rest of the photos from that day are here.)

Which then probably gets back to what Garmin might be planning here. I suspect this is two-part. First, as with any number of other sports tech sensors, pieces that used to be only possible in larger form factors can now be placed in much smaller wearables (wrist or elsewhere). Perhaps with Garmin’s advanced manufacturing capabilities, there’s some possibilities for smaller-scale muscle oxygen sensor designs. And with that, more scale given Garmin’s distribution abilities.

Likewise, and probably more likely, acquiring Moxy effectively combats someone like Whoop acquiring Moxy for the patents. I’d have to guess that Whoop would be the primary entity interested in Moxy, and given Whoop’s propensity to sue other companies these days, the preventative cost to acquire Moxy would almost certainly be cheaper than the legal cost to defend something down the road. Plus, see the next section in this post.

What happens to the Moxy user base now remains an outstanding question. Again, it’s very unlike Garmin to not issue a press release, let alone have the acquiring company assure their own user base. The good news, though, for the Moxy user base is that the device isn’t dependent on some server platform somewhere, unless they were using the Moxy Portal. But Moxy themselves (during the purchasing phase) gives you a dozen other options, some of which are totally free (and very advanced). But again, there’s nothing to say that Garmin is shutting that down today (or ever).

In any case, I figured a quick post was worthwhile in the long 12+ year arc of me covering Moxy from inception to…well…retirement?

Garmin Gets Sued For Funsies:

Welcome to last Friday, which was just like any other day of the week that Garmin gets sued on. Like most big companies in America, Garmin gets sued for all manner of things, with the vast majority of these suits being quickly dismissed. Most of the time, it’s patent trolls, and occasionally, it’s individuals that believe they’ve been wronged (and sometimes, they have).

This past Friday though, a mildly interesting patent suit came forth. This one from a company/patent owner that has made this claim before (IOENGINE), against a wide number of much larger companies, including PayPal, Imation, Ingenico, Roku, and now both Samsung and Garmin. I’m sure they’ve sued others as well. At a basic level, many of the claims follow typical patent troll behavior. The most notable case here was the PayPal one (1:18-cv-00452), which stretched on for nearly 8 years before IOEngine lost on virtually every count, and then had the remainder dismissed.

But IOENGINE is trying again.

Now, the rough claim here in both the new Garmin & Samsung cases is centered around a 2004-era patent that covers how to tunnel data between two points. It’s literally so broad that the suit covers all sorts of random scenarios, like picking a Fenix E and a Fenix 5 as the two main examples of infringement, and then from there citing totally random data sync examples, such as copying Physio TrueUp data from a device to Garmin Connect. It’s kinda all over the place.

(Also, this is the first time ever the Fenix E has been chosen for anything, so I’m guessing it feels pretty excited even if its name is being used in vain.)

For those geeks in the crowd, here’s the main claim of infringement:

At a high level, the above would best be described as “this is how computing works”.

As with many things in the patent lawsuit realm these days, it’s mind-boggling that you could even have a patent for such a basic premise. But they must be really confident in having something special here. After all, as broad as this claim is, it could be applied to just about any company, in theory. Why on earth they’d choose Garmin (or even Samsung) to fight is beyond me, given how successful Garmin is in countering patent-troll lawsuits. But hey, here we are.

In any case, I’ve flagged this one to watch. As always, Garmin has gotten more and more entertaining in their court-filed rebuttals over the past year. As evidenced by the Suunto smack-down and countersuit from earlier this year (that case continues to plod along, in case you were curious). Certainly Garmin’s lawyers might have their reasons for that TGIF legal flair; I suspect a key piece of expanding their rebuttals to be as strong as they are is to publicly dissuade others from filing lawsuits. As much fun as it might be for Garmin’s lawyers to play whack-a-mole, the reality is that it costs a lot of money and time.

With that, thanks for reading!

entry.title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs Apple Watch Series 12: Every Difference Detailed!
entry.content:
<span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span>

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Series 12 watches are both incredibly similar, and surprisingly different – depending on your perspective. Yes, at a high level, the Ultra 4 is bigger (with a bigger battery), better GPS, satellite messaging, emergency siren, deeper dive capabilities, and plenty more. But at the same time, the two units share virtually every software feature – even things like the new Max Extended battery mode launched this year, Audio Intelligence, the internal processors, and more.

Thus, this list is all about helping you figure out what’s the same, and what’s different – and most critically: Whether those specific things matter to you.

You can also check out my full Apple Watch Ultra 4 In-Depth Review here, and Apple Watch Series 12 In-Depth Review.

Still, since the announcement of both watches, I’ve been wearing them side-by-side. Or rather, one per wrist, to see exactly how they differ. As a result, I’ve gathered 50+ features and how they compare. Some of these are big-ticket (or obvious) ones, like battery capacity differences and extra buttons. While others are more subtle, such as the differences in the speakers and microphones. Or how the display panels differ.

With that, let’s dive right into it!

The Pricing:

For most people, the price will be the main deciding factor. It’s also honestly the simplest one: The Ultra 4 is essentially double the price of the Series 12, at least at the base model. Once you start getting into bigger sizes though, and cellular, and other case types (like ceramic), the price difference quickly evaporates.

Apple Watch Series 12 Aluminum (42mm): $399USD
Apple Watch Series 12 Aluminum (46mm): $449USD
Apple Watch Ultra 4 (Titanium): $799USD (5G feature included)

Note that for the Apple Watch Series 12 Titanium or Series 12 Ceramic editions, those are only available with cellular. And for the Ultra 4, that comes with cellular as the only option.

Speaking of which, on the Series 12, if you want the cellular editions, they are:

Apple Watch Series 12 Aluminum (42mm 5G/cellular): $499
Apple Watch Series 12 Aluminum (46mm 5G/cellular): $549
Apple Watch Series 12 Titanium (42mm cellular): $699
Apple Watch Series 12 Titanium (46mm cellular): $749
Apple Watch Series 12 Ceramic (42mm cellular): $899
Apple Watch Series 12 Ceramic (46mm cellular): $949

As with most years, there are a slate of new bands for all the new units, both the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. In the case of the Series 12, that includes new Nike bands, and in the case of the Ultra 4, that includes new fabric bands and new translucent ocean bands. In most of this review I’ve been wearing the Black Titanium Ultra 4 with the purple Trail band. While the Series 12 I’ve been wearing is the 46mm bronze one.

So with the financial bits out of the way, let’s dive right into the differences beyond the wallet.

The Hardware Differences:

While software can change over time, the hardware won’t. Thus, everything in this section will be the way it is forever with your watch. And honestly, that’s where almost all of the differences are. As always when purchasing, try and decide whether or not a feature actually matters to you today/now, versus something that maybe-kinda-sorta might matter, versus something that you really wish you had.

Meaning, for me I’ll take the bigger battery life of the Ultra 4 over the swankier titanium case or ceramic case on a Series 12, for essentially the same price. Whereas my wife would choose the opposite.

In any case, here we go:

– Ultra 4 has a 49mm case size; Series 12 comes in either a 42mm or 46mm case size
– Ultra 4 stock case is titanium, whereas Series 12 base case is aluminum (with both Titanium & Ceramic case options at a premium price)
– Ultra 4 has a dedicated ‘Action’ button for quick actions
– Ultra 4 has ‘Precision Start’ for workout modes, versus 3-second countdown in Series 12
– Ultra 4 has satellite messaging capability (emergency SOS, text messages, FindMy location sharing)
– Ultra 4 has cellular built-in on all models, whereas Series 12 only in certain models
– Ultra 4 gets ~2.5 days battery life in the real world, Series 12 gets ~1-1.5 days (or 84hrs vs 38hrs in Low Power Mode. Officially, the regular battery life is 50 hours and 24 hours.
– Ultra 4 has GPS battery life of 18 hours, Series 12 is 10 hours
– Ultra 4 has GPS ‘Extended’ battery life of 25 hours, Series 12 is unclaimed
– Ultra 4 has GPS ‘Max Extended’ battery life of 45 hours, Series 12 is unclaimed.
– Ultra 4 has depth gauge to 40m/131ft, Series 12 to only 6m/20ft
– Ultra 4 has depth gauge certified for scuba diving (and meets EN13319 standard), Series 12 does not
– Ultra 4 has water resistance to 100m, versus 50m for Series 12
– Ultra 4 has 86dB emergency siren, Series 12 does not
– Ultra 4 has multiband/dual-frequency GPS/GNSS, Series 12 has regular GPS/GNSS
– Ultra 4 has three microphones, versus Series 12 has one microphone
– Ultra 4 has dual speakers, Series 12 has a single speaker (but there’s no audible difference in my tests)
– Ultra 4 has a sapphire crystal display (as do Series 12 titanium models), and Series 12 base (aluminium models) have CeramicShield 2, which Apple says is 60% tougher than the Ion-X glass on the Series 11.
– Ultra 4 display max brightness is 3,000 nits, Series 12 max brightness is 2,000 nits
– Ultra 4 display area is a smidge bigger at 1,245sq mm, vs 1196sq mm (46mm) and 970sqmm (42mm)
– Ultra 4 has a fully flat screen display top, whereas Series 12 has glass curves on edges
– Ultra 4 case weight is 63g (natural/black), versus 38-52g (46mm), and 32-42g (42mm)
– Ultra 4 case thickness is 12mm, versus 9.7mm for Series 12
– Ultra 4 case has button guard around Digital Crown & Button, Series 12 does not
– Ultra 4 has been validated to MIL-STD 810H standards, Series 12 has not
– Ultra 4 has an operating temperature of –4° to 113° F (–20° to 45° C), whereas Series 12 is 32° to 95° F (0° to 35° C)
– Ultra 4 has an expanded altimeter range of -1,600ft to 29,500ft (-500m to 9,000m), whereas Series 12 is 0 feet to 10,000 feet (0m to 3000m)
– Ultra 4 has a ceramic & zirconia crystal back case, Series 12 has an aluminum or titanium with a zirconia back case
– Ultra 4 Black has a protective DLC coating on the titanium, whereas neither Ultra 4 (natural/grey) nor Series 12 have DLC
– Ultra 4 fast charges to 80% in 45 minutes, but Series 12 does 80% in 30 minutes
– Ultra 4 fast charges to 18hrs worth in 15 minutes, but Series 12 does 12hrs in 15 minutes
– Both Ultra 4 & Series 12 can do 10hrs of sleep data in 5 minutes of charging

Most of these are self-explanatory, but a few might need some additional explanation/expansion:

– Two-way Satellite Messaging: This was introduced in the Ultra 3, and includes basically three core features. The first is emergency SOS via satellite (if outside of cellular range), the second is text messaging via satellite, and lastly, the ability to update your FindMy location via satellite. This does have some coverage limitations; currently, about 17 countries are supported for Emergency SOS & FindMy (the US, Canada, and most of Europe). However, for iMessage support, it doesn’t support Europe – just United States, Canada, Mexico, and Japan.

– 1 Mic vs 3 Mics: The Series 12 has a single mic and then uses the S11 SIP chipset to do audio voice isolation when calling from the watch, despite having only a single microphone. Whereas the Ultra 4 has three mics, so it can do the majority of that in hardware, but it will still take advantage of the just-added S11 SIP as well to improve that even further. Additionally, with these three microphones, it can do wind cancellation better.

– 1 Speaker vs 2 Speakers: Both watches can play music back these days (without headphones), as well as, of course, a wide variety of other tones/notifications/sounds. Now, despite the Series 12 only having a single speaker, it seemed just as loud for music in my side-by-side tests as the Ultra 4. There was no apparent difference in quality in my test either. You can see the decibel testing side-by-side in my video.

– Multiband/Dual-Frequency GPS vs Regular GPS: There’s nobody who will dive into GPS accuracy testing as deeply (or stupidly) as I do. In most of my tests, these are mostly a wash. Still, if you’re a bit of a nitpicker (like me), there’s definitely a difference between the Ultra 4 (with multiband) and the Series 12 (without it), where the Series 12 will occasionally be just offset or slightly incorrect. It’s rarely a big deal or meaningful, but it is something you can notice.

– Case Thickness: I just want to put this somewhere, but neither the Series 12 nor the Ultra 4 changed external case dimensions this year. So those remain the same as last year, with obviously the Ultra 4 being chunkier than the Series 12 (per the exact specs above). Note that the case thickness excludes the optical HR sensor bump.

– Display Differences: Both displays have the same LTPO3 OLED display introduced first on the Series 10, and now on both Ultra 4 & Series 12 (there were no display changes this year for either watch). This improves so-called off-angle viewing. However, the Ultra 4 has a 3,000 nit display, whereas the Series 12 has a 2,000 nit display. Let’s be clear: Both displays are well beyond overkill for even the sunniest of days (I live on an island in the Mediterranean), you won’t have any issues seeing either. The only notable difference related to the display is that the Ultra has a flat-display cover (lens), whereas the Series 12 has a domed display cover. But I don’t see any difference in real-world visibility either way there.

The official dimensions for the units are:

Series 12 (42mm): 374 by 446 pixels (989 sq mm display area)
Series 12 (46mm): 416 by 496 pixels (1220 sq mm display area)
Ultra 4 (49mm): 422 by 514 pixels (1245 sq mm display area)

When it comes to battery life, the TLDR is the Ultra 4 will get you 2-ish days, whereas the Series 12 will get you 1 strong day. At least in normal smartwatch mode. It’s as simple as that. Both received slight battery increases this year, in sports mode, via the new ‘Extended’ and ‘Max Extended’ modes. As well as slight increases in GPS battery life over last year (from 8-10 hours on Series 12, and from 14 to 18 hours on Ultra 4)

As for the GPS battery life, here are the specs per Apple:

Apple Watch Series 12: 10 hours outdoors GPS (they don’t publish Extended GPS power specs)
Apple Watch Ultra 4: 18 hours outdoors GPS, 25 hours Extended mode GPS, 45 Hours Max Extended GPS mode

Thus far in my testing of both units, the battery claims are holding (at least for regular GPS modes). I’ve covered this in my Ultra 4 In-Depth Review, and will do the same in my upcoming Series 12 In-Depth Review.

The Software Differences:

There are very few differences here, but there are a couple:

– Ultra 4 has Modular & Waypoints watch face, Series 12 does not
– Ultra 4 watch face has night mode (goes to a red coloring), Series 12 does not
– Ultra 4 allows up to 7 data fields per sport mode setting, whereas Series 12 allows 6 fields. Note this includes the time in the upper right corner
– Ultra 4 has Precision Start (using the Action button), though I’d argue that’s a software feature and not really a hardware feature, hence why I’m including it in both places

Again, this excludes software features dependent on hardware features from the previous section. For example, scuba diving modes require the better depth gauge of the Ultra 4, and satellite messaging requires the redesigned antenna of the Ultra 4, and so on…

Beyond that, it’s all identical across the board.

Things That Are The Same:

One could basically surmise that everything else is the same, and that’s essentially true. Nonetheless, I want to call many of these out, just to illustrate that they are indeed, the same:

– Both run WatchOS 27
– Both have the new heart rate sensing system, which is identical
– Both support the new Audio Intelligence features of Instant Shazam, Sound Recognition, and then later this year Siri Recap and Siri Rewind
– Both have the new HRV recording features
– Both have the new Readiness Scores
– Both get access to all the new Apple Health app features that are coming here shortly.
– Both models have full access to Workout Buddy, and all the other sports features
– Both have offline Siri introduced with the S9 chipset (and now on S11 chipset too)
– Both have features like Double Tap and Wrist Flick
– Both have Blood Oxygen capability
– Both have ECG, Sleep Apnea features, wrist temperature, and all other health metrics
– Both have the Sleep Score, and Hypertension Detection features
– Both have all the same sport modes (as listed in the Workout app)
– Both can do snorkeling via the Depth gauge (and Oceanic+ app), but only Ultra 4 does full diving
– Both have the Compass app, Backtrack, Offline Maps, etc (these are all WatchOS features)
– Both can play back music on their speakers
– Both have a minimum display brightness of 1 nit
– Both have an LTPO wide-angle viewing display, just different top-glass & sizes
– Both have 64GB of internal storage
– Both have a 4-core Neural engine (S11)
– Both have the S11 SIP (chipset)
– Both units have a secondary antenna that they can use for low-signal cases
– Both have a water temperature sensor
– Both units come with a wide variety of stock/base bands, even fabric ones as default options

See, there ya go, it’s not too messy!

As with last year, some of you might ask my preference – and it’s relatively simple: I use the Ultra watches over the Series watches. The reasoning is mostly battery-focused, and simply having to charge one less thing (in my gigantic pile of things). Secondarily, I do appreciate at least the option of having Emergency SOS on my wrist, even if the iMessage piece doesn’t really work for me (yet?) here in Europe.

With that – thanks for reading!

entry.title: Amazfit T-Rex Dual Solar Hands-On: AMOLED meets Solar?!?
entry.content:
Amazfit took one for the team. That’s probably the best way to describe the new Amazfit T-Rex Dual Solar, which features a combined AMOLED display with not just one solar panel, but two entirely different solar panel systems. Since the first AMOLED displays came out years ago, people have been asking for companies (well, asking for Garmin, I suppose) to make a Fenix AMOLED Solar combo-dish.

But Garmin has long resisted that idea, stating simply that the power equation just didn’t make sense, and that it was better to take that extra space and simply stick a bigger battery in there. Still, many fans really, really, really wanted an AMOLED watch with solar panels nonetheless, doubting Garmin’s team of battery and solar engineers.

To which Amazfit said: Hold my beer. Actually, two beers.

And thus, here we are, with probably one of the geekiest watches of 2026, including both a front and rear solar panel (yes, on the back). And yes, we finally got an AMOLED-Solar hookup, rejoice!

Let’s dive into it, as I suspect it might be the only one we’ll ever see. Still, I’m all here for the geeky!

Some Quick Spec Differences:

Now, the Amazfit T-Rex Dual Solar is essentially a T-Rex Ultra 2 watch from a features standpoint, though there are some notable hardware differences. Still, Amazfit says it’s basically a twin to that watch.

Key Amazfit T-Rex Dual Solar vs the Amazfit T-Rex Ultra 2 differences:

– Has a smaller 660mAh battery vs 870mAh on Ultra 2
– Has a smaller 1.3” AMOLED display vs 1.5” AMOLED display on Ultra 2
– Has deeper depth gauge allowance (50m, vs 45m on Ultra 2)
– Waterproofing spec of case is still 100m
– Has a white/red LED flashlight, vs white/green LED flashlight on Ultra 2
– Gains new LiveShare feature, though all Amazfit watches will gain this via App
– $649/649EUR ($100 more than Ultra 2 at $549/549EUR)

And then, from an overall standpoint, here’s how the Amazfit models differ – including notably the battery claims:

And then here’s a much deeper chart of battery details on the solar model:

At this point, it’s probably worthwhile noting that Amazfit says they aren’t trying to compete here with a MIP-based Fenix MIP/Solar model. Instead, they say that most people want that AMOLED screen, but the idea here is to offer that option to provide some extra battery gains via solar, if required.

The Solar Panel Features:

Now, I want to point out up front that while it’s clear the overall solar-to-gain equation here simply doesn’t work for any real-world scenario, what Amazfit has done around the user interface of the solar gains is so much better and more detailed than Garmin’s watch-based solar units. So, if there’s anything to take away from this watch, it’s probably that.

Still, we have to take a moment to appreciate what Amazfit has put together here, as I’m not aware of any other watch on the market with both front and rear solar panels. So, let’s start there, on the back of the watch.

This panel is obviously normally against your wrist, but the idea is that you can take the watch off your wrist during a break in a long adventure (such as a lunch break, or after you’ve hiked many hours and are done for the day), and then face it towards the sun. At which point, you’re gathering double the solar gains as the front panel. Amazfit says that the solar area is pretty close to double that of the front area, and equally, the gains are 2x that of the front panel.

There are a few things you’ll notice as a result of this. First, they’ve shifted the charging connector to the side of the watch, and gone with a different connector than all their other current-gen watches. This is a little bit of a bummer if you have something like their Amazfit Helio band for sleep instead (since now you need two different charging connectors), but I wouldn’t say it’s a deal breaker.

Next, is that with this rear-facing design, there’s a new ‘Solar Boost’ mode that gets activated when the rear-facing panel starts getting sun. You can technically also manually enable it, but practically speaking, once this thing ‘sees the light’, it pretty much activates immediately. That Solar Boost mode makes the rest of the watch inaccessible until you exit it.

Now, the main downside here is simply that the watch overheats in this flipped over mode really darn quick. Like, within 10 minutes quick in the toaster temperatures I live in (80-90°F/27-32°C). And once it does that, it doesn’t make any solar gains at all. Amazfit says in cooler temperatures (such as the top of a mountain), it’ll likely keep from overheating but still get plenty of solar juice.

Still, if you do the math here, even if I have to switch to the front panel, just 21 minutes of that is better than 10 minutes of the back panel, which then shuts off until it cools down. Nonetheless, that back panel, and the curvature into the optical HR sensor is super pretty/stunnng:

And certainly, in temperatures cooler than mine, it sounds like you won’t get overheating at all (such as in cooler alpine mountain temps).

When it comes to seeing those product gains, there’s a dedicated Solar widget. This widget starts off with a glance within the widget roll. From there, upon opening, you’ll see the last 4-hour graph, and the current/instant inbound power. Again, this is *NOT* total gains for the 4-hour duration, but rather the exact to-the-second current solar gains coming in:

However, that chart actually shows more than you might realize. It actually has two colors on it, such as below, showing both front panel and rear panel solar gains separately. I like this. Below you can see this where it was a bit breezier in the afternoon, and I managed to keep it cool enough:

In any case, below that you’ve got the Solar Index, which looks at the quality of the solar gains coming in. Again, you’ll notice the color coding.

And then finally, within this widget, there are gains materialized in the three core modes: Regular smartwatch mode, battery saver mode, and the watch-only mode (just time basically). I *really* like this, as it’s something that Garmin doesn’t do on their watches. Not so much the different modes, but they don’t show the battery gains (in days).

Note, however, this doesn’t account for your battery ‘losses’. Meaning, if you ‘lost’ 4 days of battery just by using the watch but gained 2 days from solar, you’re still at a 2-day loss. Also note, along the top you can change the timeframe 1d/7d/30d, which again, I rather like.

And all of this is also visible on the companion app too:

Next, back on the watch itself, there are a few final things I want to mention. First is that when you flip over the watch, it’ll automatically engage the rear panel. But, you can manually control that in the settings:

Likewise, you can manually force it into Solar Boost mode from the settings:

In the same place that you can force Battery Saver mode, as with any other Amazfit watch.

Now, for lack of anywhere else to mention it, the watch can indeed charge from completely dead (0%) using purely solar. So if you manage to kill it off, and then have a bunch of time to sit in the sun, it can jump-start it and get you back and cooking.

Ok, with that, let’s talk about some workouts, as well as general results from non-workout activity.

Real World Workouts and Gains:

I feel like every section here kinda has to start out with a ‘even if this boat sinks, at least they went down trying’. And in that case, I appreciate that Amazfit is pretty honest with the minimal gains you’d expect to see here in real-life conditions. In many ways, the solar aspects of this watch are really only useful if you’re in a situation where you’ve got pure blue-sky sun all day, but not using much of the watch itself beyond basic time operations.

Day out in sun with mostly back gains (roughly 6 hours):

Start day battery: 53% (9:45AM)
End day battery: 55% (3:15PM)
Note: Numerous overheat messages, don’t have battery % photos after 3PM, so just left gains above from 9-3PM

Another day out in the sun with mostly back gains (roughly 12 hours on back). I didn’t take a photo in the morning, but did take an evening photo with the solar gains listed:

Total time gained: 2.8d Smartwatch time
Total time gained: 8.4d Battery saver time
Total time gained: 14.0d Watch time
Note: Numerous overheat messages

And in fact, looking at each day I left it outside, it was almost always 2.5-3.0-days in smartwatch time gains via solar, regardless of whether it was front or back. That’s because on the back, it’d basically overheat (oscillating back and forth), whereas on the front it didn’t overheat (only once, I think), but gained less solar power (half the amount, but did it for consistently longer). But at the same time, it was also losing that amount each day in battery life, so it kinda ended up roughly a wash if I didn’t wear it at all (which defeats the point of the watch).

Next, a few different workouts. For fun, let’s actually start in the dark for an hour at night on a bike alongside my wife, who was doing a run for about 80 minutes. In this case, we can baseline the power draw (not always-on display, gesture-based, default GPS mode), with no solar gains:

Start battery: 45%
Duration: 1hr 20 mins
End battery: 42%
Loss per hour: ~2%
Note: At night, GPS enabled, no always-on display (gesture-based)

Next, we’ve got a 1-hour run yesterday. In this case, there were some initial scattered thin clouds, and I was getting about 30-40lux through that; then that single thin cloud moved on, and I was around 70-80lux. Obviously, occasional trees or body blockage, though I had tried to structure the route so that my wrist was mostly facing the sun.

Start battery: 43%
Duration: 1hr
End day battery: 41%
Loss per hour: 2%
Note: No overheat messages, generally quite sunny conditions, GPS enabled, no always-on display

Next, I went out for a 2-hour ride on a blue-sky sunny day. I even structured the route so that I had the watch facing the sun as much as possible for the ‘slower’ portions (gravel/ascending), and then more mixed for some of the faster descents.

However, for reasons that aren’t clear, it looks like the solar panel entirely failed to charge here. You can see that when I returned, the exact times the workout was going on, it showed zero solar power:

Amazfit is digging into it. There’s some theory that perhaps the automatic solar panel selection algorithm failed here and was actually activating the rear panel (they can’t operate concurrently), which would have been against my wrist. Still, even the moment the ride was saved/ended, solar charging resumed normally. Either way, here are those numbers:

Start battery: 51%
Duration: 2 hrs 12 mins
End battery: 46%
Loss per hour: ~2%
Note: No overheat messages, but also, seemingly no solar gains

Finally, here’s another nearly 3-hour ride, with mixed coverage. In this case, it was blue-sky sunny out, but some of the route and stoppage time had tree coverage, which reduced solar gains. But again, such is the real world:

Start battery: 16%
Duration: 2 hrs 57 mins
End battery: 10%
Loss per hour: ~2%
Note: No overheat messages, mixed sun conditions (due to trees)

Anyways, I’ll likely add in some more workouts with more data, though I think at this point there’s enough detail to get a relatively clear picture of battery gains from solar across various scenarios. Obviously, if you have less sun than I do, you’ll get less battery gains. Equally, if you have colder weather that’s still as sunny, you might get more gains from off-wrist scenarios.

Wrap-Up:

As I alluded to at the beginning, the Amazfit T-Rex Dual Solar is in many ways the very definition of form over function. But that’s OK. It delivered on the oft-asked request to merge together an AMOLED screen with solar, gains and battery life be damned.

And look – I appreciate Amazfit’s willingness to try and make this work. I think the back solar panel, and how it blends into the base of the optical heart rate sensor bump, looks great. Admittedly, I’ll almost never see it on my wrist, but hey, that’s kinda like having fancy underwear. Likewise, I really like Amazfit’s way of showing the battery gains in the solar widget. Though, I do wish they showed total cumulative lux hours throughout the day, similar to Garmin. But otherwise, the solar gains widget is just way more data practical/useful on Amazfit than Garmin.

Still, we can’t overlook the obvious here: The solar gains are, even in a best-case, crazy-sunny, stick-your-watch-outside-all-day scenario…basically negligible. In the days I stuck it outside all day, I gained a mere 2-3% of battery life. But equally, remember on those days I wasn’t wearing the watch (which would have consumed far more power with the display turning on optical HR sensors, algorithms, etc…). Once you put it on your wrist, as I showed during a GPS workout with body vs sun position/trees/etc… you quickly get to a near wash in battery gains between a sunny day and a night activity.

In other words, the reason AMOLED+SOLAR was resisted historically is because it simply didn’t make sense. You had to shrink your battery considerably in order to fit all the extra solar pieces in there (just like Amazfit did). And then you have to shrink your display to fit the solar ring around that (which Amazfit did). And then once you did those things, with the power draw of AMOLED, you were left with a watch that actually gets less battery life than what you started with (which is where Amazfit lands now). And that ignores that it’s also more expensive.

Nonetheless, as I said, first attempts don’t always work out. But hopefully Amazfit takes another swing at this down the road. I certainly don’t expect Amazfit to venture into MIP-based displays, especially as that market further dwindles. But I do like seeing a company push the bounds of things, even if it’s not quite a product I would buy.

With that, thanks for reading!
